subtitle: Star Citizen's technical model, GTA's climb, Hearts of Iron at the corporate scale. Information is the scarce commodity and attention is the one you cannot buy. Codename Ledger; the name is undecided.

milestones.title: Prototype spike (delivered)
milestones.goal: Answer the two questions that could have killed the project: can a deterministic belief simulation be made legible, and can one engineer render a real-scale planet you fly to and from without a loading screen.
milestones.gate: Both answered yes. out/world-dump.txt traces a corporate collapse back four causes and shows two NPCs disagreeing for legible reasons; the client flies orbit to ground to orbit continuously, with water, weather and a town.

gateChecks.check: A dump of the running world traces a corporate collapse back four causes.
Two NPCs hold different beliefs about the same fact, for reasons the dump explains.
The client flies orbit to ground to orbit with no loading screen.
Water, weather and a settlement are present and rendered.

milestones.title: Architecture and the split
milestones.goal: Turn the spike into a structure before building anything complex on it. Cargo workspace, Unreal modules, the god-files split along real seams, and a build that refuses to compile a layering violation.
milestones.gate: No source file over 500 lines; every UE module declares three or fewer dependencies except LedgerGame; adding an illegal dependency fails CI with a named rule; the scripted flight renders identically to before the split.

gateChecks.check: No source file exceeds 500 lines.
Every module declares three or fewer project dependencies, except the composition root.
A dependency pointing up the layering fails the build, naming the rule.
Captures match the committed reference within the perceptual tolerance.
The flight model's tests pass with no world, actor or frame involved.

milestones.title: The world as an Unreal project
milestones.goal: Stop being a tech demo that only runs inside the editor. A real level, materials that are assets rather than node graphs rebuilt on every launch, and a mechanism that turns a generator into a saved asset with Nanite, LODs, collision and instancing -- so that everything generated after this is a first-class Unreal asset and not a procedural mesh with none of it.
milestones.gate: A packaged build, with no editor present, flies the scripted flight and renders within the perceptual tolerance of the editor build.

gateChecks.check: A packaged build with no editor present flies the scripted flight to completion.
Its captures match the committed references within the perceptual tolerance.
Its frame-time report is no worse than the editor build's.
No material in the project is constructed at runtime; every one is a saved asset.
The project opens on its own map, not on an engine map.
One command regenerates every generated asset from its definition.
A second run leaves version-controlled generated assets byte-identical; derived ones are checked by settings and render, because Unreal packages embed GUIDs.
A generated hull is a static mesh with Nanite, a full LOD chain, matching collision and a distance field.
Draw count for a settlement's scattered props is independent of the instance count.
A generated asset with no definition behind it is reported by a validator, naming the file.
The terrain component comparison is written down with measured generation, upload and draw costs for each candidate.
A packaged build shows no shader compilation stall on first sight of any material.

milestones.title: Terrain to production standard
milestones.goal: The terrain stops being a spike. Stable LOD with no popping, collision wherever a body can be, caves and overhangs, biome-driven material blending, and a streaming budget that holds at speed.
milestones.gate: Fly a 200 km transect at 300 m and at 900 m/s: no holes, no popping that reads as a seam, no frame over 16 ms, and collision present under the ship at every point along it.

gateChecks.check: A 200 km transect at 300 m altitude reports zero unfilled patches.
The same transect at 900 m/s reports zero unfilled patches.
A downward trace hits terrain on every frame of that transect.
No frame exceeds 16.7 ms during the transect.
Walking a ridge at 2 m/s across four LOD boundaries shows no vertex movement.
Three biomes meet on one slope with no visible blend band.
No texture repetition is identifiable at any distance in the biome capture.
Every river reaches the sea or a basin; none flows uphill.
A cave is entered, traversed and exited with collision and lighting correct throughout.
One command turns a generated asset into a contact sheet, at fixed exposure, with the camera provably outside the geometry.
Two consecutive runs of the turntable agree within the stated tolerance, worst single channel.
Ten thousand scatter instances render inside the frame budget, placed identically across runs.

milestones.title: Close-range surface fidelity
milestones.goal: Make the ground convincing at walking distance and out to the horizon. The source scans are already photogrammetry at 4K; what is missing is displacement, variation across scales, an end to the visible tiling grid, and geometry fine enough to carry any of it.
milestones.gate: Twelve side-by-side pairs against real photographs at 2 m, 20 m and 200 m, each with a written verdict; no terrain triangle edge over 40 px while standing; no visible tiling period in an overhead capture; and the 200 km transect still holds its frame budget.

gateChecks.check: Twelve side-by-side pairs against real photographs at 2 m, 20 m and 200 m, each with a written verdict.
At least three of those verdicts name a specific remaining deficiency.
Standing on flat ground, no terrain quad exceeds 40 px at 1920x1080 measured at 20 m.
A 50 m profile of the drawn mesh deviates from a fitted line by at least 15 cm RMS.
Adjacent LOD depths agree to within 25 cm, so the ground does not re-form as the rings sweep.
An overhead capture shows no autocorrelation peak at the tiling period above the noise floor.
Each of albedo, normal, roughness, AO and height is shown, isolated and at pinned exposure, to be the map the manifest names.
A capture at 3 m shows stones whose silhouettes break the horizon line behind them.
Four biomes at eye height look like four different places, and the closest pair differs by more than 15 of 255.
The frame time cost of the whole milestone is attributed to geometry, material and scatter separately.
The scripted flight reports zero unfilled patches at the resolution recorded in its own report.

milestones.title: Planetary bodies and orbital mechanics
milestones.goal: A solar system that moves. Planets, moons, rings and stations on real orbits, axial tilt, rotation, day and night, seasons, eclipses — all deterministic from seed and all consistent between the map and the sky.
milestones.gate: Stand on a surface and watch a moon rise, transit and set on the schedule the orbital model predicts. Fly to it. The ephemeris and the sky agree to the arcminute.

gateChecks.check: A moon rises, transits and sets within one arcminute of the ephemeris prediction.
Sky and ephemeris agree to the arcminute at 100 sampled times and locations.
Positions computed forward from zero and directly at time t agree to sub-metre over a simulated century.
A moon's phase matches the sun-moon-observer geometry from any body in the system.
An eclipse predicted by the ephemeris is observable from the surface at the predicted time.
Illuminance at each planet matches the inverse-square prediction.
Landing on a moon uses the same terrain code path, with correct low gravity and no atmosphere.
A system regenerates identically from its seed in a second process.

milestones.title: Atmosphere, weather and environment
milestones.goal: Air that behaves. Layered atmospheres per body, volumetric weather that moves and matters, storms with real wind fields, temperature and pressure as physical quantities the rest of the game reads.
milestones.gate: Fly into a storm front: visibility, wind loading on the ship and cockpit audio all change together, and the same storm is visible from orbit in the place the weather model puts it.

gateChecks.check: Flying into a storm front changes visibility, wind loading and audio together.
The same storm is visible from orbit at the position the weather model gives it.
A storm tracked over a simulated week follows a coherent path and reproduces from its seed.
Three cloud decks resolve at the altitudes the atmosphere profile predicts.
Rain falls below the freezing level and snow above it, at the boundary the lapse rate puts it.
Fog fills a valley at dawn, is absent on the ridge above, and is invisible from orbit.
A steep re-entry heats and a shallow one does not, from the density-velocity integral.
Worst-case weather costs no more than 4 ms of GPU time.
Wind speed changes and all five consumers respond within one second.

milestones.title: Ship framework: hulls, components, subsystems
milestones.goal: Ships as systems, not props. A component graph — power plant, thrusters, fuel, cooling, avionics, life support, shields — with real dependencies, damage that propagates through it, and hulls assembled from parts.
milestones.gate: Shoot out a power coupling and watch thrusters on that bus go dead, heat climb, and the affected systems degrade in an order the component graph explains. Repair it and the ship comes back.

gateChecks.check: Destroying a power coupling kills exactly the components downstream of it and nothing else.
Heat climbs and affected systems degrade in the order the component graph explains.
Repairing the coupling restores the ship to its stated condition.
Overloading a bus sheds load in the configured priority order.
Loading cargo on one side changes handling measurably in the predicted direction.
Fuel burned over a flight matches thrust integrated over the same flight.
A cold start brings systems up in dependency order; skipping a step prevents the next.
A hull breach vents the compartment behind it and not the rest of the ship.
Every instrument traces to a component reading; a failed sensor makes its gauge unavailable, not wrong.
Shutting down non-essential systems measurably reduces detection range.
A new ship is one data file plus art, requiring no recompile.

milestones.title: Flight model in vacuum and in air
milestones.goal: Flight worth doing. Six-degree thruster allocation solved rather than faked, aerodynamic lift and drag in atmosphere, control surfaces, landing gear, gravity, and the transition between the two regimes.
milestones.gate: Take off from a pad, fly aerodynamically to another continent, exit the atmosphere, manoeuvre in vacuum, re-enter with heating and buffeting, and land on the pad you left. Cockpit view and instruments only.

gateChecks.check: Disabling one thruster makes the allocator compensate, losing authority in the axis the geometry predicts.
Angular response matches the inertia tensor; off-axis thrust produces the torque the geometry gives.
A winged ship glides unpowered in atmosphere and does not in vacuum.
A deliberate stall departs controlled flight and standard recovery inputs recover it.
A re-entry from vacuum to sea level shows no discontinuity in forces at any altitude.
A hard landing compresses the gear and can damage it; a shallow one does not.
Switching flight-assist mode changes only the controller; the physics underneath is provably identical.
Auto-land places a ship on a pad in wind, repeatably, from any approach.
A full flight is completable on instruments alone with the external view disabled.
Pad to another continent, to vacuum, through re-entry, back to the same pad — cockpit view only.
All three input devices produce identical commanded forces for equivalent input.
A recorded flight replays to an identical trajectory.

milestones.title: Seamless travel across a system
milestones.goal: Distance made crossable without a loading screen. Origin rebasing, multi-scale rendering from centimetres to astronomical units, and a high-speed travel mode with a real spool, a real interruption, and a real cost.
milestones.gate: Fly from a planet's surface to a moon of another planet in one continuous shot, with no loading screen, no cut, and no precision artefact anywhere along the path.

gateChecks.check: At one AU from origin, a one-millimetre movement is still one millimetre, for every actor and particle system.
No z-fighting between a hand-held object and a planet in the same frame.
Surface of one planet to a moon of another in one continuous shot, no loading screen and no cut.
No frame exceeds 16.7 ms anywhere along that path.
No allocation spike over budget anywhere along that path.
A ship a thousand kilometres away is a dot; approaching it loses no state and shows no pop.
A ship in transit is pulled out at the position and velocity the interdiction model predicts.
Estimated and actual travel time agree within five percent over twenty sampled routes.
A twenty-minute transit ends with position error inside tolerance and no jitter at any point.

milestones.title: Physics at scale and local grids
milestones.goal: The hardest engine problem in the project: walking around inside a ship that is itself moving at speed near a rotating planet. Nested reference frames, which Chaos does not have.
milestones.gate: Walk from the back of a ship to its cockpit while it accelerates, rolls and flies through atmosphere. Set a cup down and it stays on the table. Step out onto a landing pad on a rotating planet and inherit the right frame.

gateChecks.check: Walking stern to cockpit while the ship accelerates, rolls and crosses an atmosphere works without sliding.
An object set on a table inside a manoeuvring ship stays on the table.
Stepping from a pad onto a hovering ship and back shows no jolt, no launch and no lost velocity.
An object at rest inside a manoeuvring ship stays at rest relative to the ship, at any reachable speed.
A dropped object inside a spinning station lands where the rotating frame predicts, not directly below.
Stepping onto a landing pad on a rotating planet inherits the correct frame.
A projectile at any modelled speed always hits the surface it should, over ten thousand trials.
Two levels of grid nesting are stable; the limit is enforced with a clear error.
A recorded physics scenario replays identically at 30, 60 and 144 frames a second.
Ten active grids with two hundred bodies each stays inside the physics budget.

milestones.title: Embodiment and animation
milestones.goal: A body worth being in. Character controller with real momentum, full-body IK, procedural foot and hand placement, first and third person from one skeleton, interaction, seats, ladders, EVA.
milestones.gate: Walk out of a room, climb a ladder, cross a pad in wind, board a ship, take a seat, fly, and get out again — one continuous shot, no cut, no teleport, no animation that slides.

gateChecks.check: Room, ladder, pad in wind, ship, seat, flight, and out again — one continuous shot with no cut or teleport.
No locomotion transition slides the feet, at any speed or direction change.
Feet land on the ground that is there, at its angle, on stairs, slopes and debris.
The same controller produces correct movement at 0.16 g, 1 g and 1.5 g with no special-cased animation.
Crossing a compartment in zero gravity conserves momentum throughout.
First person shows the same body doing the same thing a third-person camera shows.
Boarding a hovering ship and taking the seat involves no teleport and no cut.
A new interactable is one data declaration and inherits highlighting, reach and animation.
Stepping into vacuum without a sealed suit kills on the modelled schedule, with warnings from the suit's components.
Every character mesh and animation clip has a manifest entry naming its source and licence.
An animation asset on disk with no manifest entry fails the build, naming the file.
Two hundred visible characters stay inside the animation budget with no visible LOD switch.

milestones.title: Interiors and modular architecture
milestones.goal: Insides. Ship interiors, station interiors and building interiors built from a modular kit, generated where they should be generated and authored where they should be authored, with no door that is a loading screen.
milestones.gate: Walk from a city street into a building, up through it, out onto a roof pad, into a docked ship and through it to the cockpit, with no load, no fade, and no drop below the frame budget.

gateChecks.check: Street, building, up through it, roof pad, docked ship, cockpit — no load, no fade.
No frame during that traversal exceeds 16.7 ms.
An interior assembled from the kit has no gap, no z-fight at any seam, and correct collision.
Twenty generated interiors of one purpose are all navigable with no unreachable room.
Every component in a ship's graph has a physical location inside it that can be walked to.
A habitat on an airless world has an airlock and visible life support; the same archetype on a temperate world does not.
A hundred walkable interiors in view cost no more than the handful visible through their openings.
Cutting power to a building darkens its interior and brings up emergency lighting on its own reserve.
Two ships with different component fits produce different cockpits with no hand editing.
Every readout in a generated cockpit traces to a component in that ship's graph; an orphan readout fails the build.
Every control is reachable from the seated position without blocking the sightline to the horizon.
An automated traversal agent covers every reachable point of ten generated interiors without getting stuck.

milestones.title: Rendering fidelity
milestones.goal: The look. A real PBR material pipeline, lighting that works from a lit cockpit at night to a sunlit dune, volumetrics, decals, wear, post, and the LOD and impostor chain that lets it survive at range.
milestones.gate: Side by side against reference footage at three distances and three lighting conditions, a stranger cannot immediately sort ours from theirs on material and lighting alone.

gateChecks.check: Shown twelve pairs of stills — ours and reference footage, at three distances and three lighting conditions, in random order — five people who have not seen the project identify ours correctly no more than 60% of the time.
Every material in the project conforms to the documented PBR standard.
A single hull material produces a clean ship and a filthy one from parameters alone.
No shadow acne, peter-panning or cascade seam at cockpit, landscape or planetary scale.
Flying from a dark hangar into daylight adapts smoothly with no overshoot and no clipped scene.
No ghosting on cockpit instruments during rapid motion; no shimmer on terrain at any distance.
No LOD transition is visible at any distance for any asset class.
A character at conversation distance holds up in three lighting conditions.
A cockpit at dawn, noon and night each hold up, with legible instruments in all three.
The same asset with the wear layer disabled and enabled, at identical framing and exposure, is captured as one pair.
Every post effect has a measured cost and a documented reason; the chain is inside its budget.

milestones.title: Asset pipeline and world content
milestones.goal: A way to get content in that is not a person placing things by hand -- and under ADR-0005 there is no other way, because nothing is bought and no artist is assumed. Generators for hulls, plating, surface detail, markings, buildings, settlements and biomes; validation, LOD generation and material assignment over their output; and the variation framework that stops all of it reading as the same thing repeated.
milestones.gate: Add a new ship and a new biome end to end through the pipeline, with no manual step outside the tool, and both appear correctly at every LOD.

gateChecks.check: A new ship goes from mesh to flyable with interiors, through the pipeline, with no manual step outside the tool.
A new biome is added the same way and appears correctly at every LOD.
A deliberately broken asset is rejected at import with a message naming the problem.
An imported asset arrives with a full LOD chain and collision matching its silhouette, unattended.
A generated building's exterior openings correspond exactly to its interior layout.
One archetype placed on four environments produces four structurally different buildings from one definition.
A complete star system is authored end to end without editing source.
Memory stays inside budget through a two-hour session visiting every content type.
A packaged build runs the full technical slice with no editor present.
Three ships of visibly different design language come from three data files with no mesh editing.
No hull plate spans a hard curvature break, and no marking lies across a seam.
Greeble density correlates with component placement rather than being uniform noise.
A measured repetition score over a generated street and a generated interior falls below the stated threshold.
No asset anywhere in the project was purchased; every one is generated or carries a free-licence manifest entry.
Every texture in the project has a recorded source and licence.

milestones.title: Performance and optimisation
milestones.goal: Budgets met with everything running at once. Rendering, streaming, physics and memory, at the densities the design actually asks for.
milestones.gate: Sixty frames a second with a full city, a docked ship interior and traffic in view, no frame over 16 ms, and a two-hour session with no memory growth.

gateChecks.check: Sixty frames a second with a full city, a docked ship interior and traffic in view.
No frame exceeds 16.7 ms in any of the five fixed scenarios.
A two-hour session ends with the memory profile it started with.
Draw calls in the densest scene are below budget with no visual change.
Visible triangle count in a city falls by an order of magnitude under culling, with no visual change.
Every render pass is inside its budget in the worst scenario.
A full traversal of the slice shows no frame over 16.7 ms.
Three quality levels hit their target frame rate on three hardware profiles.
A deliberate performance regression fails CI.

milestones.title: Technical vertical slice
milestones.goal: Prove the model. One system, one planet, one moon, one city, one station, three ships — everything above running together and holding up under an hour of unscripted play.
milestones.gate: An hour of free play with no loading screen, no crash, no frame over 16 ms, and nothing that reads as placeholder. This is the milestone the whole technical plan exists to reach.

gateChecks.check: An hour of unscripted free play with no crash.
No loading screen at any point during that hour.
No frame over 16.7 ms during that hour.
An automated audit reports zero placeholder assets in the slice.
Ten hours of mixed play with no crash and no state corruption.
Five external testers complete a free-play session; observations recorded and triaged.
Every transition in the slice — door, ladder, seat, airlock, dock, frame change — is reviewed and none reported as rough.
An ADR records what the technical model proved, what it did not, and what it forces on the simulation plan.

milestones.title: Simulation core and determinism
milestones.goal: The substrate the living world is written against: event log, reducer contract, snapshots, replay, and a harness that proves reproducibility before there is anything complicated to reproduce.
milestones.gate: Replay a 100,000-tick log twice from one seed and diff the snapshots byte for byte. CI fails on divergence and names the first differing tick.

gateChecks.check: A 100,000-tick log replayed twice from one seed produces byte-identical snapshots.
CI fails on divergence and names the first differing tick.
Snapshot-plus-tail and full replay agree byte for byte at 100,000 ticks.
Introducing a float into any authoritative struct fails a test.
Renaming an event struct does not change its wire id.
A log written against schema version 1 replays under version 2.
A one-year log compacts and still replays to the same hash.
No reducer is reachable except through a validated command.
Any event walks back to a root cause with no domain-specific code.
The client renders identically from a live sim and from a replay of it.

milestones.title: Agent framework
milestones.goal: The longest simulation milestone, and the one every other system reduces to. Needs, goals, planning, schedules, competence, loyalty — and agents that act on their own beliefs rather than on world state.
milestones.gate: Run 500 agents for 30 simulated days. Any one agent's whole history is explained by its needs and its beliefs, with no appeal to world state it never observed, and two agents holding different beliefs act differently.

gateChecks.check: 500 agents run 30 simulated days without error.
Any agent's full history is explained by its needs and beliefs, with no appeal to unobserved world state.
A test proves the planner cannot reach world state.
Two agents holding different beliefs about one fact demonstrably act differently.
An agent with a false belief plans as though it were true.
An agent with a motive to deceive does so, and the false belief propagates and is later contradicted.
Two agents of different competence attempting one action produce measurably different outcome distributions.
An agent demoted to statistical detail and promoted back has a consistent history and an invisible transition.
Ten thousand agents are created, tracked and retired over a simulated year with no leak or orphan.
Any agent's current action is explained in one screen with no code reading.
Two hundred simulated agents are visible as characters going about traceable business, inside budget.

milestones.title: Organisation framework
milestones.goal: Membership, roles, holdings, treasury, doctrine and span of control. A player organisation and an NPC organisation are the same type, founded through the same API, subject to the same drift.
milestones.gate: Over-extend an organisation and watch drift appear as subordinates pursuing their own goals — with no code path in the org layer that asks whether the owner is a player.

gateChecks.check: An over-extended organisation exhibits drift as subordinates pursuing their own goals.
Drift emerges from agent goals, with no code in the org layer producing it directly.
No branch anywhere in the org crate reads a player flag.
A player organisation is founded through the same API an NPC one is.
The chartering authority's disposition changes measurably as a result of chartering.
Two organisations with identical assets and different doctrine produce measurably different action distributions.
No reputation field exists; two organisations demonstrably hold different beliefs about a third.
An agent defects to a rival when the offer beats their position on their own terms, and the org learns of it late.
Oversight demand and supply are computable, and their ratio predicts the observed drift rate.

milestones.title: Economy and logistics
milestones.goal: Goods, markets, production, contracts and convoys. Materials that have to physically arrive, which is what turns a build order into a logistics problem and a convoy into a target.
milestones.gate: A supply shock in one system moves prices three systems away with a lag that matches travel time. Ninety days with no negative inventory and no money created outside a mint event.

gateChecks.check: A supply shock moves prices three systems away with a lag matching travel time.
Ninety simulated days with no negative inventory.
No money created or destroyed outside an explicit mint or sink event.
A three-deep production chain runs for a simulated year with conservation holding at every stage.
Two markets in one system hold different prices for one good, explained by supply and transport cost.
A shipment's arrival matches the route's travel time; destroying it removes the goods from the destination's supply.
A breached contract has consequences propagating as belief and obligation, not as a number changing.
Ten one-year runs from different seeds end with functioning economies and no runaway.

milestones.title: Sites, construction and city life
milestones.goal: Claims, construction projects, four utility networks, condition that degrades, maintenance crews that respond, and a first-person tell for every mechanic.
milestones.gate: Build the same habitat archetype on a temperate world and an airless storm moon: different composition and cost from one definition. Cut power to a district and watch life support fail, crews respond, and people put masks on.

gateChecks.check: One habitat archetype on a temperate world and an airless storm moon produces different composition, cost and maintenance rate.
Cutting a power node causes exactly the downstream failures the graph predicts, in the predicted order.
A district that loses life support evacuates, and its population appears elsewhere rather than vanishing.
All six first-person tells are observable by walking through a running city.
Each tell is driven by simulation state rather than triggered for display.
A crew fed a false belief about a fault location goes to the wrong district, and the right one stays dark.
An understaffed organisation's backlog appears as public contracts; taking one clears the work order.
A construction project is identifiable by sight at four stages of completion.
A project on a remote world is delayed by a late convoy and by a storm, both traceable.
A site's environment matches what the renderer and weather model report at that location.

milestones.title: Power, threat and coalitions
milestones.goal: The ceiling. Threat models built on belief rather than truth, alarm that rises with believed power and falls with dependency, and coalitions that form because several organisations independently reached one conclusion.
milestones.gate: Grow an organisation until rivals independently cross alarm and form a coalition against it. Feed one member a fabricated belief about another and watch the coalition fracture.

gateChecks.check: A coalition forms in a scenario with no code that decides a coalition should form.
Each member can state why it joined, from its own threat model.
A fabricated belief fed to one member fractures the coalition.
A coalition dissolves both because its target fell below threshold and because a partner rose above one.
A test proves the threat model cannot reach ground truth.
Alarm responds correctly to each of its five inputs in isolation.
Each of the four counterplays — hide, bribe, fracture, be useful — demonstrably breaks or prevents a coalition.
Establishing a supply relationship measurably lowers the customer's alarm; severing it raises it.
Observable event rate scales with organisation size; a large one cannot reach a small one's concealment.
Twenty one-year runs produce neither a runaway hegemon nor a frozen balance.

milestones.title: Missions and directives
milestones.goal: Missions generated from tension rather than authored, with stakes that are changes to the world. Directives: standing orders resolved by agents whether or not anyone is watching.
milestones.gate: Every generated mission traces to a named tension between real parties and none has a stake that is only money. A directive left alone for a simulated week resolves through subordinates, correctly or otherwise.

gateChecks.check: Every generated mission traces to a named tension between real parties.
No generated mission has a stake that is only a payment.
Removing a tension removes the missions generated from it.
A directive left alone for a simulated week resolves through subordinates.
A directive given to an incompetent or disloyal delegate produces a different outcome, explained by the agent.
The same task done personally and by directive differ in all four stated ways, each measurable.
A player directive produces a mission on the open board for an NPC, with no special code path.
The same tension produces different offers to agents of different standing.
A one-year run produces missions across all tension classes, none exceeding a stated share.

milestones.title: Presence and Command
milestones.goal: The second lens. A map of what your organisation is doing, built from what your people have reported rather than from ground truth, with directives issued from it and your body still standing where you left it.
milestones.gate: Open Command mid-flight: the world does not pause and the ship does not stop. A report three days stale is visibly stale, and a fact nobody has observed does not appear at all.

gateChecks.check: Opening Command mid-flight does not pause the world or stop the ship.
A test proves the Command data path cannot reach world state.
A fact nobody has observed does not appear on the map.
A report three days stale is visibly stale and its source is inspectable.
Two contradictory reports are both shown with their sources rather than one silently winning.
Every directive type is issuable from Command and resolves identically to one issued programmatically.
A hostile agent can find and act on the player's body while Command is open.
A hundred simultaneous events produce a legible summary rather than a hundred notifications.

milestones.title: The living world, integrated
milestones.goal: Everything at once, for a long time, without supervision. This is where the frameworks either compose or they do not.
milestones.gate: Run one simulated year unattended. No runaway monopoly, no dead economy, no organisation with a thousand ships, no agent stuck in a loop, and a dump that still explains itself.

gateChecks.check: One simulated year runs unattended with no crash and no deadlock.
No unbounded quantity anywhere in that year.
No runaway monopoly and no dead economy at the end of it.
No organisation exceeds a stated ceiling on fleet size.
No agent is stuck in a loop.
A collapse anywhere in the year-old world is traceable back four causes from the dump.
The same engagement fought in person and resolved in Command produces outcomes from one distribution.
The simulation tick stays inside budget with fifty thousand agents across thirty-two systems.
A one-year world saves and reloads in under thirty seconds with a matching hash.
Killing the simulation mid-session degrades the client visibly and recovers with no invented facts.

milestones.title: Vertical slice: nothing to coalition
milestones.goal: The game. Arrive with nothing, take work, build a crew, charter an organisation, claim ground, build on it, and grow until the galaxy decides you are the problem.
milestones.gate: A player who has never seen the game goes from nothing to a chartered organisation to a coalition forming against them, in one save, with no tutorial explaining any of the systems.

gateChecks.check: A player who has never seen the game reaches a chartered organisation with no tutorial.
A coalition forms against that player's organisation in ordinary play.
The player can see from Command why it formed.
Playtesters find at least two of the four counterplays unprompted.
A new player has a reason to move within sixty seconds of gaining control.
A player can earn a living from generated work alone for three sessions without repetition becoming visible.
Playtesters reach the point of using Command without being told to.
Median time from nothing to the coalition falls inside the intended band across ten playtests.
Ten testers complete the arc; findings recorded, triaged, and either fixed or explicitly deferred.

tasks.title: Wave displacement and shoreline foam
tasks.detail: Crossed Gerstner-style trains, damped in the shallows.
tasks.acceptance: Waves are visible from 200 m and flatten against the shore.

notes.text: Wave phase is Frac(AbsoluteWorldPosition / wavelength), not a plain divide. At a 6371 km radius a world coordinate is ~6.4e8 and float32 has no fractional part left there, so sin() of it returns a staircase. Frac on an absolute world position is the one operation LWC keeps exact. It also rules out the camera-relative position the terrain material uses, which would make the wave field swim with the camera.

First pass keyed foam off a shore band 8 m deep with pow(x,4): a shallow inlet is almost entirely under 8 m, so the whole lagoon went white and read as pack ice. 3 m and pow(x,6) gives a surf line instead. The band doubles as wave damping, so the same number decides where the swell flattens.

notes.text: The post-process material failed to compile because SceneTexture outputs float4 and the murk constant is float3 — Lerp between them is not a legal expression. UE answers a failed material with one warning and the default material, and for a post-process blendable that means WorldGridMaterial gets drawn over the entire screen. Second time this failure mode has cost a debugging round; grep the log for 'Failed to compile Material' after every material change.

Murk is applied after tonemapping, so its constant is a final screen value, not a radiance. A physically sensible 0.018 blue rendered as a black screen — there is no exposure left at that point in the pipeline to lift it. 0.05/0.17/0.21 reads as water.

Underwater the sea floor is unlit: the water sheet is section 1 of the same procedural mesh as the terrain, the component casts shadows, and there is no per-section shadow control. Everything below the waterline sits in the water's own shadow. Splitting water into its own component per patch would fix it and also skip collision cooking for water. Blocks anything that wants a visible seabed.

notes.text: The seabed was pow(depth, 0.75) — a concave curve, steepest at the shore and flattening outward. That is a bathymetric profile inside out: real ocean floor is a nearly flat shelf, an abrupt break around 140 m, a steep slope to a few kilometres, then an abyssal plain flatter than anything on land. Replaced with those four segments as an explicit piecewise function of the offshore parameter.

The first transect showed no break at all and I nearly retuned the thresholds on the strength of it. The thresholds were fine — the coast search picks its seaward direction by probing six kilometres, which distinguishes water from land and not a basin from a lagoon, so the line ran down the length of an archipelago. Scoring 32 directions on the mean depth of the outer half found open ocean and the break appeared where the profile says it should.

notes.text: First version cached at upload time, holding a copy of every patch currently drawn. With ~1000 visible patches at ~700 KB that is most of a gigabyte duplicating what the mesh components already hold, and the budget evicted useful entries to make room for live ones: 4 hits against 4870 generations, 4484 evictions. The cache must hold only what is NOT on screen. Entries are now taken in ReleaseSection and removed again on reuse.

Storing FProcMeshSection rather than the generator's parallel arrays. Taking a copy on release is one memcpy of an interleaved buffer and putting it back is SetProcMeshSection, so nothing is converted in either direction and the arrays the worker produced can still be moved straight into the component.

The first sweep test swept 18 km in 4 seconds — Mach 26. It covered new ground the whole time, generated 13,615 patches and measured streaming throughput, not the cache. A cache can only be tested by a path that repeats: 3 km at 300 m/s gives 86 percent reuse.

notes.text: Two causes, neither of them the prefetch. The second bake had silently failed to write -- SavePackage will not overwrite an existing file and SAVE_NoError was hiding the failure -- so the comparison was of each file against itself. That is the same self-confirming measurement the turntable's camera check made, and I made it again the same day. Found while wiring T419's one-command regeneration, which ran the bake a second time and reported 'could not write the package' for all three. The bake now deletes the previous file first and reports the real save result. What is actually true: Unreal packages embed GUIDs and are NOT byte-reproducible. Of 73 generated assets, exactly one is stable across regenerations -- Maps/Ledger.umap, which is the only one tracked in version control, so nothing churns. The materials and textures are derived and gitignored, and their equivalence is established by their settings read back off the assets and by the render matching the reference, not by their bytes.

tasks.title: Asset generation as an editor commandlet
tasks.detail: The mechanism the generators of ADR-0005 plug into: a generator is a function from parameters to geometry, and this is what runs it offline, names the package, saves it, and records what produced it. One command regenerates everything from source, so a change to a generator is a rebuild rather than an afternoon of clicking.

notes.text: tools/generate_assets.py regenerates every generated asset in the project from its definition, in one command: the level, the 69 imported surface textures, and the three baked materials. 'python tools/generate_assets.py' takes about a minute; --only <step> runs one; --list says what each step makes and why. Index kept at docs/comparisons/project-level/generated-assets.json. EVIDENCE: a full run reports 'level ok -- the map exists, surfaces ok -- 69 textures imported, materials ok -- VERDICT: PASS', and a second full run does the same rather than failing on the first. Two bugs it found, both the same shape -- a generator that worked exactly once. make_level.py called new_level, which refuses to overwrite, so every run after the first failed to validate the destination. The material bake called SavePackage, which will not overwrite an existing file, and SAVE_NoError was swallowing the failure -- which is also how T418's byte-identical evidence came to be wrong, since the unwritten files compared equal to themselves. Both now delete first. Steps are judged BY THEIR ARTIFACT, not by exit code: both Unreal entry points return non-zero on a successful run -- the import commandlet validates an unused global block and fails on it, and the editor's shutdown does not reliably return zero -- so a generator that trusts exit codes either fails on success or succeeds on failure. Provenance: each baked material carries Ledger.Generator, Ledger.Source and Ledger.Command as Unreal metadata, so it travels with the asset and shows in the details panel. No timestamp, deliberately: an asset that embeds when it was made can never be compared against a re-run.

tasks.title: Static mesh output with Nanite, LODs and collision
tasks.detail: What the commandlet actually emits. Nanite enabled where it belongs, automatic LOD chains, simplified collision matching the silhouette, and distance-field generation. None of this is available to a procedural mesh and all of it is free once the output is a static mesh, which is the whole argument of ADR-0006 in one task.
tasks.acceptance: A generated hull comes out as a static mesh with Nanite on, a full LOD chain, collision matching its silhouette and a mesh distance field, with no manual step.

notes.text: The ship hull is now a static mesh asset at /Game/Meshes/SM_ShipHull, baked by 'UnrealEditor.exe <project> -game -bakemeshes' and by tools/generate_assets.py as a step. LedgerMesh::Bake takes the same FLedgerMeshBuilder arrays the runtime uses and hands them to Unreal's own static mesh build, so the shape is described once and has two destinations. EVIDENCE, read back from a FRESH PROCESS rather than from the process that set it -- 'I set the flag' and 'the asset has it' are different claims: tools/verify_meshes.py opens the saved asset and reports '144 tris, nanite on, lods 1, collision yes, dist field yes, by LedgerMesh::Bake'. VERDICT PASS. Kept at docs/comparisons/project-level/verify-meshes.txt. Both things this unlocks were previously impossible: Nanite cannot be enabled on a procedural mesh component at all, and the mesh distance field is what Lumen's software tracing needs -- its absence across the whole project is why Lumen had to be forced onto hardware ray tracing in the first place. On 'a full LOD chain': the asset has one source model, and that is the right answer for a Nanite mesh rather than a shortfall. Nanite does LOD per cluster, so a hand-built chain would be both redundant and, on 144 triangles, meaningless. Said plainly rather than counted as met. NOT DONE: only the hull is baked. The settlement's buildings and trees are still runtime procedural meshes, because they want a material instance per colour and that is the instancing task.

[2026-09-09] CORRECTION. This task reported 'nanite on' for SM_ShipHull, read back from the saved asset -- which was true of the asset and false of the running game. Both the editor and the packaged build were on Shader Model 5, and Nanite requires SM6, so Nanite was configured and not running. Found by packaging: a packaged build states its feature level in the first hundred lines of its log, and the editor had been saying the same thing for two days. DefaultGraphicsRHI is DX12 with PCD3D_SM6 now, and the editor reports 'Using Highest Feature Level of D3D12: SM6' with raytracing=1. The asset-level verification in this task was correct as far as it went; it just did not go as far as asking whether the feature was available at all.

tasks.title: Instanced rendering for repeated and scattered assets
tasks.detail: Three hundred and forty-two trees are three hundred and forty-two procedural mesh components today, each with its own draw and its own generation cost on the game thread. Once assets are static meshes they instance, and a forest becomes one draw. The scatter framework in M02 decides where they go; this decides what they are placed as.
tasks.acceptance: A settlement's trees and props render as instanced draws, the draw count is independent of the instance count, and the measured game-thread cost of placing them falls against the current build.

notes.text: Trees are now instances of a baked static mesh: two UHierarchicalInstancedStaticMeshComponents, 174 and 168 instances, replacing a single merged procedural mesh of 43,092 runtime-generated vertices. MEASURED, steady state, two consecutive runs: settlement build 3.0 and 3.2 ms against a 5.4 ms baseline, of which loading both tree meshes is 1.2-1.4 ms and placing all 342 instances is 0.0 ms. Draw count is independent of instance count by construction -- two components whether there are 342 trees or 3,420. Hierarchical rather than plain instanced, so a group of trees behind a hill is culled as a cluster; the merged mesh was one primitive, drawn whole or not at all. First readings were 38.9 ms and then 8.8 ms and I nearly recorded the task as a regression on them; both were first-load-after-bake, where the asset's derived data is built on demand. THREE WRONG GUESSES before the trees rendered correctly, each looking like the last: they came back black, and I blamed a missing material assignment, then an sRGB decode on the vertex colours, then Nanite. The actual causes were two. A material without bUsedWithInstancedStaticMeshes is silently swapped for the default on an instanced component, and BuildFromMeshDescriptions creates no material slots at all -- so SetMaterial(0, ...) succeeded, reported the material back, and drew nothing. The component was asked what it had and answered '0 material slots'. Vertex colours were then dropped entirely in favour of a material slot each for trunk and canopy, which is how this is normally done and depends on none of it. A correction to the task's own text: it claimed 342 trees were 342 procedural mesh components. They were one.

tasks.title: Asset layout, naming and ownership in the content tree
tasks.detail: Where generated assets live, what they are called, and how a stale one is found. Boring, and the alternative is a content directory nobody can navigate in two years and a set of orphans nobody dares delete.
tasks.acceptance: Every asset's package path is derived from its definition rather than typed, and a generated asset with no definition behind it is reported by a validator naming the file.

notes.text: Every asset's package path is derived from its definition -- /Game/Materials, /Game/Meshes, /Game/Surfaces and /Game/Maps, each root owned by one generator -- and tools/verify_assets.py walks the whole content tree and fails on anything without a Ledger.Generator tag or outside a known root. Evidence: 76 assets checked, VERDICT PASS, kept at docs/comparisons/project-level/verify-assets.txt. Materials and meshes tag themselves as they are baked. The 69 textures are imported by Unreal's own commandlet, which knows nothing about this project, so tools/tag_surfaces.py writes their source and licence on afterwards FROM THE MANIFEST rather than from a second copy of the same facts. The validator caught itself first: its opening version reported '/Game/Maps 0' and passed, having never looked at the level, because get_assets_by_path does not return World assets. A validator that quietly checks nothing is worse than none, because it is believed. ONE HONEST EXCEPTION, written down rather than waved through: the level cannot record its generator in the asset. Package metadata set before a map save is dropped and metadata set afterwards is not persisted by save_asset -- both were tried, and an actor tag on the world settings did not take either. Its provenance is kept beside it in build/make-level.txt and the validator checks that line, so the level is held to the rule rather than exempted from it.

tasks.title: Terrain component type, measured rather than assumed
tasks.detail: After this milestone the terrain is the only runtime-generated geometry left, and it owns the game-thread cost failing the frame budget: 20 to 31 ms through every low-altitude phase against 16.7, with the GPU at 5 to 9. UProceduralMeshComponent was the prototype's choice and has never been compared against anything. Measure it against the alternatives on generation, upload and draw cost before deciding to keep it.
tasks.acceptance: A written comparison of at least two component types over the same flight, with generation, upload and draw cost measured for each, and a decision recorded with its numbers.

notes.text: Measured. UProceduralMeshComponent kept: over the same flight it uploads 121,918 patches to the static backend's 8,212, and finishes with 6 holes against 2,584. The static run's p99 is lower (29.0 vs 33.1 ms) only because it is drawing a starved world -- compare_captures puts the worst channel difference between the two runs at 199 against a limit of 16.

The comparison also produced the answer to a question nobody had asked: the terrain tick's cost was never the upload. Breaking ALedgerPlanet::Tick into phases put the LOD tree walk at 24 ms and upload at 7. UpdateTree was taking a full fractal elevation sample per visited node per frame for a value that never changes; caching it on the node took the ridge sweep from 18.8 ms of terrain to 11.2 and the flight p99 from 43.3 to 35.1.

tasks.title: Shader compilation and PSO caching
tasks.detail: Building material graphs at runtime means compiling shaders at runtime, which is a stall the moment anything new comes into view. Once materials are assets their shaders cook, and the pipeline state objects need collecting so that first sight of a surface is not a hitch.
tasks.acceptance: A packaged build shows no compilation stall on first sight of any material, and a first run's frame-time trace matches a second run's within the stated tolerance.

notes.text: PSO precaching is on and takes effect; the two D3D12 driver disk caches cannot be enabled from project config -- read-only CVars read before it is applied, still logging r.D3D12.PSO.DiskCache=0 under both RendererSettings and SystemSettings. 28 PSOPrecacheState:Missed in cold AND warm runs, identical, so precaching is not covering them. 973 frames over the stall threshold, worst 116.5 ms. First run vs second: overall 17.2 then 17.8 ms (noise), but the town phase 17.0 then 20.0 -- 18% apart with nothing changed, so the run-to-run tolerance is not demonstrable yet. Needs ConsoleVariables.ini or a command-line route for the read-only CVars, and a stall attribution pass to find what the 973 actually are. Reports in docs/comparisons/packaged/.

The two D3D12 driver disk caches are unreachable, not merely unset. Tried RendererSettings, SystemSettings, [ConsoleVariables] (the earliest project-owned section, applied in PreInit) and -dpcvars on the command line; all four give 'CVar deferred - dummy variable created' followed by 'Not using pipeline state disk cache per r.D3D12.PSO.DiskCache=0'. The RHI reads the value in the pass that registers it. The lines are out of DefaultEngine.ini rather than sitting there looking like a setting somebody chose. They were also the wrong lever: they are the driver's copy, not the engine's, and the engine's answer is a recorded .upipelinecache shipped with the build.

Run-to-run half of the acceptance now measurable, because the fixture is reproducible: cold and warm packaged runs under -useFixedTimeStep agree to within 2% on every phase mean (overall 16.4 vs 16.6 ms) and 12% on p99. The previous attempt had the town phase 18% apart with nothing changed; that was the free-running fixture. Still failing: 34 PSOPrecacheState:Missed, IDENTICAL cold and warm, so precaching is not covering them and nothing carries them between runs. Also: the 22 stalls in the cold run land on the capture timestamps -- taking a screenshot stalls its own frame and the recorder counts it, so stall attribution has to exclude capture frames first. Evidence in docs/comparisons/packaged/pso/.
unblocked

Stall attribution done. The recorder now drops frames while a screenshot is outstanding -- a fixed two-frame skip was tried first and removed only nine of twenty-two, because the request is served whenever the render thread gets to it, and picking a larger number until the list looked clean would have been picking the answer. Count 22 -> 12. What is left lands on t=124 (coast teleport), t=132 (underwater teleport) and t=140 (start of the climb): the frames where the camera moves somewhere new or the tree collapses. None coincides with a precache miss. So the 34 misses are 30 in the warm-up window and 4 in flight, and the flight's stalls are the terrain's cache-copy problem rather than shader compilation. Remaining work for the acceptance is a recorded .upipelinecache to take the 34 to zero.

Recording pipeline built end to end: stable keys from the cook, a clean flight exit so the recording flushes, 38 recorded PSOs -> 82 stable -> a 38-PSO binary cache at Content/PipelineCaches/Windows/Ledger_PCD3D_SM6.stable.upipelinecache, which is the exact path and name FPipelineFileCacheManager constructs. The runtime never opens it -- no FShaderPipelineCache lines in the log at all -- and the miss count is unchanged at 34. STOPPED DELIBERATELY: PSOPrecacheState:Missed is reported by the PSO precaching system and the bundled cache is a different mechanism, so a working cache might not move that counter. Four package-and-fly cycles went into a number that may not be connected to the change. Prerequisite for finishing is a meter that measures the bundled cache; the other candidate is that nothing calls OpenPipelineFileCache.

MET, both halves. Cause of the last wall: BuildCookRun DELETES loose non-asset files from Content/ during the cook, so the cache built into Content/PipelineCaches/Windows was gone by staging -- the log said 'Could not open FPipelineCacheFile' naming the exact path, under a string I had not grepped for. tools/pipeline_cache.py builds from the committed .spc and installs into the staged build after packaging. PSOPrecacheState:Missed 34 -> 0, cache opened with 38 entries, precompile finished with no jobs remaining. Second half: tolerance stated for the first time at 10% on phase means; eight of eleven phases agree to 0.0% between two cold runs, worst 6.3% on underwater, the one phase whose settle wait times out. Correction: I had claimed the miss counter might be the wrong meter for a bundled cache. It was the right meter.

tasks.title: Package the technical slice and run it without the editor
tasks.detail: The narrow version of what M12 does properly later: prove it packages and runs at all. Today it cannot, and every milestone spent adding content on top of a build that has never shipped once is a milestone spent finding out later.
tasks.acceptance: A packaged Windows build launches with no editor present, flies the scripted flight, and writes its captures and frame-time report.

notes.text: A packaged Windows build launches with no editor present, flies the whole scripted flight, and writes its eight captures and its frame-time report. build/package/Windows/Ledger.exe, 901 MB, packaged by RunUAT BuildCookRun. Evidence kept in docs/comparisons/packaged/. Two real failures found, which is what packaging was for. FIRST: nothing was cooked. Generated assets are loaded by path string at runtime, so no asset in the project references them and the cooker never saw them -- the first packaged build came up reporting 'SkipPackage: /Game/Materials/M_Terrain, the package to load does not exist on disk or in the loader' for every material and mesh, and rendered a planet with no material. Fixed by naming the directories in DirectoriesToAlwaysCook. SECOND: the flat material could not be baked at all, because it took its colour as a constant and the settlement wants a different one per building -- so buildings, trees and the hull rendered as black cut-outs on correctly textured ground. Its colour and roughness are parameters now, one baked asset with a dynamic instance per user, and LedgerSurfaceCooked.cpp is empty of fallbacks for the first time. NOT MET, and it belongs to the milestone gate rather than this task: the packaged captures do not match the editor's within tolerance, worst channel 193. And the reason is worth more than the mismatch -- BOTH builds report 'Using Highest Feature Level of D3D12: SM5' and raytracing=0. Nanite and Lumen hardware ray tracing both require SM6, so neither has been running since I enabled them, in either build. Every claim I have made about Lumen HWRT and about Nanite being on the hull needs re-checking against that.

tasks.title: Write down the asset creation strategy
tasks.detail: What is baked, what is streamed, what is placed, and how a new kind of thing gets added to each. ADR-0006 records the decision; this is the document somebody follows. It exists because the current architecture was never chosen -- it is what the prototype happened to do -- and the way that happens again is by leaving the choice implicit.
tasks.acceptance: A document that answers, for any new asset type, which tier it belongs in and what producing one involves, with a worked example for each of the three tiers.

notes.text: docs/asset-strategy.md. Answers, for any new asset type, which of the three tiers it belongs in and what producing one involves, with a worked example for each: a new prop and a new material for baked, a new placed actor for placed, and for streamed the honest answer that there is no example and the test is 'write down how big the file would be'. It also carries the five traps this milestone actually hit, each of which cost an afternoon and none of which is guessable: vertex colours do not survive the trip from procedural mesh to baked-and-instanced; a material without bUsedWithInstancedStaticMeshes is silently swapped for the default; BuildFromMeshDescriptions creates no material slots so SetMaterial succeeds and draws nothing; generators must be idempotent because new_level and SavePackage both refuse to overwrite; and a number taken straight after a re-bake measures the first load of freshly built derived data, which is how the settlement read 38.9 ms, then 8.8, then 3.0 with nothing changed. Plus what is and is not in version control, why .uasset files are not byte-reproducible, and a closing section naming the seams that are still open.

tasks.title: Playable proof: the packaged build flies the same flight
tasks.detail: Per ARCH Rule 6 the milestone ends with something that runs: a build with no editor, flying orbit to ground to orbit, producing captures that match the editor build.
tasks.acceptance: Captures from the packaged build match the committed references within the perceptual tolerance, and its frame-time report is no worse than the editor build's.

notes.text: Not met, and the reason is a flaw in the harness rather than in the build. Packaged against the editor's references, on the same SM6 configuration: 4 of 8 captures pass and 4 fail -- town 4.16, coast 8.26, surface 10.13, sweep 14.70, against a 2.50 limit. The four that fail are exactly the phases where the ship is moving fastest and terrain is streaming; town, the slowest, is closest to passing. CAPTURES ARE TRIGGERED ON GAME TIME, so a build with a different frame rate reaches a given timestamp having streamed a different amount of terrain, and the images differ for a reason that has nothing to do with rendering. Two builds with different performance can never match a time-triggered capture. The fix is to trigger on STATE -- altitude reached, distance travelled, patches resident -- which also makes the existing editor-to-editor comparison mean something stronger than it does now. Frame-time half of the gate: packaged overall 17.2 ms against the editor's 17.5, so the packaged build is not worse. Evidence in docs/comparisons/packaged/.

CORRECTED DIAGNOSIS. My first explanation was that captures fired before terrain had streamed, and it was wrong. Captures now wait for PendingBuilds and JobsInFlight to reach zero before firing, and seven of eight settle on the first 0.1 s poll -- the terrain was already idle. The comparison barely moved: coast 8.26 to 7.93, sweep 14.70 to 14.68, town 4.16 to 4.16. THE ACTUAL CAUSE, with evidence: the packaged run logs 926 stalls against the editor's 543, from the same seed and the same start position. The flight model integrates at a fixed 120 Hz step with a capped catch-up -- MaxStepsPerFrame 16, accumulator zeroed when capped -- so a stall DROPS simulated time rather than spiralling, which is deliberate and is what the SurvivesAHitch test protects. A build that stalls more has flown less far by any given timestamp, so a time-triggered capture photographs a different place. Nothing to do with rendering, and nothing a settle can fix. THE FIX is to trigger captures on ship state -- altitude crossed, distance travelled -- so the image is a function of where the camera is rather than of how fast the machine is. That is a rewrite of the harness's scheduling, which is timer-driven throughout, and it is worth doing because it also makes the editor-to-editor comparison mean something stronger. The settle wait is kept: it is correct on its own terms, and it is now labelled as not having been the problem.

THIRD DIAGNOSIS, and this one was tested before it was written. Both previous explanations were about the packaged build. Neither was checked against the obvious control: run the EDITOR build twice and compare it with itself. Seven of eight shots disagree, coast by a mean of 7.67 -- against the 8.26 that had been blamed on the packaged build. The fixture cannot reproduce itself, so no comparison against it meant anything. Cause: the flight is driven by game time, game time advances by however long the last frame took, so position, LOD state and Lumen history are all functions of the frame rate. -useFixedTimeStep -fps=60 takes the worst channel across the set from 128 to 21 and six of eight shots pass outright. Evidence in docs/comparisons/repeatability/.
unblocked

MET. Two causes, both found by testing rather than reasoning. (1) The fixture could not reproduce itself; -useFixedTimeStep -fps=60 pins it. (2) With it pinned, the same four shots still failed -- the four with sky in frame -- because UVolumetricCloudComponent takes its material from its own class default, nothing in the project names that asset, and the cooker never saw it. The packaged log said 'the package to load does not exist' and the build rendered a clear sky. /Engine/EngineSky added to DirectoriesToAlwaysCook. Gate now: eight of eight captures match, worst residual 0.89 against a limit of 2.50. Frame times packaged 16.6 ms mean / 27.6 p99 against the editor's 18.0 / 29.0 over 8,760 frames each -- not worse. Both still fail the 16.7 ms budget, which is the terrain work's problem and not this task's.

tasks.detail: Quixel Megascans through Fab, decided 2026-09-08. The first version of this task said the scans are free for Unreal use, which is wrong and was corrected by reading the listings: Megascans *3D assets* have a free tier that is UEFN reference-only, while Megascans *materials* are free outright under the Fab Standard License. tasks.title: Texture import pipeline for surface sets
tasks.detail: Pulled forward from M12, because sixteen sets imported by hand is sixteen chances to get a normal map's colour space wrong and one afternoon wondering why the lighting is inside out. Channel packing — roughness, ambient occlusion and height into one texture — compression settings per map type, sRGB flags, mip and streaming policy.

notes.text: tools/import_surfaces.py takes a Fab texture-set zip and needs nothing else: it reads the scan's real-world size from the bundled metadata for tiling, keeps albedo and normal, packs AO/roughness/height into one RGB texture (nine triplanar samples become six), names the maps it discards and why, and writes the manifest entry. notes.text: Two photogrammetric scans, grassy soil at its own 2 m tiling over rock cliff at 1 m, chosen by slope and interlocked by height rather than cross-faded. Captured at three distances (1.7 m, 12 m, 140 m) under two sun elevations (20 and 62 degrees) with exposure PINNED -- auto exposure exists to cancel differences in scene brightness, which is the one thing a two-lighting-condition comparison is trying to show. Frames in docs/comparisons/surface-study/. Beside the noise version: docs/comparisons/noise-before/ holds the old reference captures, and compare_captures puts the change at 4.23 structural residual on the town frame and 62 on orbit, against a 2.5 regression threshold. Frame cost measured, not assumed: GPU 5.2-8.6 ms across the low-altitude phases with Lumen on, roughly 3 ms of that being Lumen. This task recorded a GPU cost 'with Lumen on, roughly 3 ms of that being Lumen', and the commit enabling Lumen said hardware ray tracing was doing the work because software tracing needs distance fields the project has none of. tasks.title: Runtime Virtual Texture for surface composition
tasks.detail: Compose the blended surface into an RVT so the expensive blend happens once per texel rather than once per pixel, and so decals and roads have something to write into. Moved up beside the material work: it is what makes layered authored sets affordable at all.
tasks.acceptance: Terrain material cost falls measurably against the direct-blend version with no visual difference.

notes.text: Measured before building. A -flatterrain control arm swaps the surface for an untextured constant on identical geometry; the GPU difference over the same fixed-step flight is the whole budget an RVT competes for. It is at most 0.7 ms anywhere on the flight, and 0.1 and 0.0 ms in the surface and town phases where terrain fills the screen. There is nothing to recover: an RVT would add page rendering, memory on top of a 512 MB patch cache, and a cache invalidated by terrain that uploads 762 patches a second. Size is not the objection -- non-adaptive RVT gives 2.39 m/texel over a cube face, adaptive gives 9.3 mm. Evidence and the control-arm capture in docs/comparisons/terrain-material-cost/.

Blocked on a consumer, not on effort. The performance premise is measurably false -- the whole terrain material costs at most 0.7 ms, and 0.0 where terrain fills the screen. The surviving justification is that decals and roads need something to write into, and there are none yet. Revisit when the biome and settlement work needs a target, and size the RVT for the play area rather than the planet.

tasks.title: Geomorphing across LOD transitions
tasks.detail: Vertices interpolate toward their coarser position as the transition approaches, so a split is a blend rather than a jump. The current pop is small at altitude and unmissable at walking pace.
tasks.acceptance: Walk a ridge line at 2 m/s across four LOD boundaries with no visible vertex movement at any of them.

notes.text: Each vertex records where the parent LOD would put it: even positions do not move, edge-odd ones sit at the midpoint of their two even neighbours, centre-odd ones at the average of four. Only a scalar is stored, not an offset — the coarse position is the same direction at the interpolated elevation, and the chord-versus-arc error that approximation costs is a fraction of a millimetre against elevation differences of metres.

The blend is driven by the same quantity the LOD decision uses, or the two disagree and the pop moves rather than disappearing. A node collapses when its parent's projected error falls below threshold, and the parent is twice the size, so the collapse distance is 2*WorldSize*MorphScale — one number packing viewport width, field of view and the pixel threshold, set once per frame on one material instance. Nothing is per-patch: what differs per patch is baked into its vertices.

The capture comparison caught a bug I was not looking for. Three captures differed after the change, and it was not the morph — the ship fell a different distance before the first screenshot because the flight model integrated with the frame's own delta. Frame-rate-dependent physics, which my own coding standard warns about, on a run that happened to be faster than the one before it. Now fixed-step at 120 Hz with bounded catch-up. Orbit capture difference went from 24.78 to 0.03.

Determinism at a fixed step was already tested and passed; nothing asked whether two different step sizes agreed. That test now exists, plus one asserting a ten-second hitch does not become ten seconds of catch-up on one frame — which is how a stall puts a ship on the far side of a planet.
