tasks.title: Stitching for the finer-neighbour case
tasks.detail: Edge stitching currently handles a coarser neighbour. The mirror case arises whenever LOD is driven by anything other than pure distance, which it is about to be.
tasks.acceptance: A forced-depth region adjacent to a natural one shows no crack from any angle.

notes.text: Measured before building anything. Found a real bug on the way: LeafDepthAt descended to the tree's leaf, but a split node keeps its geometry until all four children have theirs, so during streaming the thing on screen is the parent at the parent's resolution while the tree below is several levels deeper. Stitch flags are computed from that function, so a patch stitched against a neighbour it was not meeting — a crack that appears under load, closes when the load passes, and is invisible in any still taken afterwards. Fixed: it now stops at whatever is drawn.

The imbalance counter itself was wrong twice over. It read 43% of all edges imbalanced on terrain with no visible crack, which was the tell. The collected leaf set contains a split parent AND its children while the children stream, so it was comparing nodes that are not both on screen. Now filtered to drawn nodes only. Unverified — needs a run.

Metric corrected twice and not yet re-measured. Whether the tree needs a balancing pass at all is still an open question, and building one before the measurement is trustworthy would be building it on a number I have already been wrong about twice.

[2026-09-08] A third reading, from the 900 m/s 200 km collision transect rather than the scripted descent: 6495 imbalanced edges against 1736 active sections, so roughly 94% of edges, worst depth gap 12. Not evidence the tree is unbalanced. At 900 m/s the camera outruns patch upload, so LeafDepthAt keeps stopping at a shallow ancestor that is still the drawn node — the deep neighbour exists in the tree and has not arrived. That is a streaming-rate fact wearing a stitching metric's clothes. The metric needs to distinguish 'the neighbour is coarser' from 'the neighbour has not uploaded yet' before any number from it means anything, and until it does, this stays blocked rather than becoming the third wrong number I build on.

tasks.title: Collision streaming with a cook budget
tasks.detail: Cooking is the expensive half of a patch. Predictive cook along the velocity vector, bounded per frame, with a guarantee rather than a hope.
tasks.acceptance: At 900 m/s at 50 m altitude, a downward trace hits terrain on every frame of a 200 km transect.

notes.text: Measured, not assumed. 200 km at 900 m/s and 50 m altitude, tracing downward every frame: 16128 frames, 0 misses, longest gap 0. out/transect.txt. Predictive cook along the velocity vector was already in place — collision is requested for any node within CollisionRadius of either the camera now or its predicted position — and this is the first run that proves it holds at speed rather than hoping. The per-frame cook budget in the task description was NOT built: worst cook cost across the whole run was 1.227 ms with ~320 nodes carrying collision, so a budget would cap a cost that never approaches a cap. Add one when cook ms starts appearing in the frame-time tail, and not before. Two bugs found running it: TransectDistance was 2e9 cm, which is 20000 km and not the 200 km its own comment claimed, a six-hour run; and the flight harness and the transect were both placing the same pawn, so neither measured anything.

tasks.title: Give the planet relief: the height function has no mountains
tasks.detail: The mountain band of the elevation function is exactly zero on ninety per cent of the land, and the whole planet tops out at 1,372 m against a configured 9 km. LedgerNoise::ErodedRidged returns (Sum / Normalisation) * 2 - 1, remapping to [-1,1] the way a signed fBm should -- but a ridged field with a continuity weight and erosion damping concentrates its energy into a few ridges, so its mean sits far below 0.5 and the remap puts most of the surface negative, where Elevation's FMath::Max(0.0, ...) deletes it. Four tasks are blocked on this and it has been living in their blocker notes; it is work in its own right. Whatever the fix -- a different pivot, an unsigned return, a renormalisation against the field's own measured distribution -- it reshapes every landform and invalidates every reference capture, which is why it is a task and not a patch.
tasks.acceptance: Ranges that read as ranges from 80 km, land reaching a decent fraction of MaxElevation, and slopes steep enough to hold scree -- measured by the existing relief and slope surveys, not by eye. The reference captures are re-adopted in the same commit and the write-up says what changed.

notes.text: Highest land 1,372 -> 2,462 m, steepest slope 57.0 -> 62.1 degrees with 1.08% of land above 30 and 0.015% above 60 where there had been none, and major ranges on the planet 2 -> 609. Two changes. ErodedRidged's [-1,1] remap assumes a mean of 0.5 and this field's is -0.49 -- measured over the land and printed by -climate -- so FMath::Max(0.0, ...) was deleting everything below the 97th percentile; RidgeStrength renormalises against the measured distribution. That reached 1,911 m and stopped, because Land^1.4 in the range mask capped it: the continent mask only reaches 0.581 and no point had a strong ridge and high land at once, since they are independent fields. Land^0.7 lets a range stand on ordinary continent. Cost, measured over the same flight: terrain game thread in the surface phase 1.28 -> 10.5 ms, GPU 7.2 -> 11.7, frame p99 31.5 -> 32.8. A flat planet was cheap. It also found a defect in T063's LOD brake -- with relief, occupancy reaches the engagement point and the loop chased itself, patch cache at 88% reuse over 158,000 hits; a dead band fixes it and -nolodbrake stays as a control arm. All twenty reference captures re-adopted. Commit 317a620, write-up in docs/comparisons/relief/.

evidence.caption: The ridge phase after the fix: a peak with a snow line, rock on the steep faces, and further ranges on the horizon. Before, this frame was a flat plain.
Highest land 1,372 -> 2,462 m; steepest slope 57.0 -> 62.1 degrees; major ranges 2 -> 609.

tasks.title: Climate model: temperature and moisture fields
tasks.detail: Latitude, altitude, prevailing wind and distance from water produce temperature and moisture as continuous functions. Biomes are read from them rather than painted, so they are consistent with the terrain that produced them.
tasks.acceptance: A pole-to-equator transect shows monotonic temperature and a rain shadow on the lee side of every major range.

notes.text: Temperature done and tested: LedgerClimate::At is a pure function, four automation tests green in ~90 ms (monotonic sea-level temperature pole to equator, lapse rate, bounded moisture, wind bands reversing). Rain shadow NOT demonstrated, and the cause is the terrain. The transect finds two major ranges on the whole planet and both are shadowed -- which is not a pass: at the base rate below, two for two happens by chance about a third of the time. Asking every wind-crossing ridge instead, 1,018 of them with each ridge's own two flanks compared, gives 56% drier on the lee. A coin toss. Two explanations were tried and both wrong: a 25 km march step wider than a ridge (cut to 7.5 km, 54% -> 50%), and a population comparison that said rising ground is WETTER (0.361 vs 0.293 over 2,600 points each) because it was measuring distance from the sea. The real reason is the relief survey: highest land on the planet is 1372 m against MaxElevation configured at 9 km, land p90 673 m. The height function uses fifteen per cent of its range and makes smooth low noise, not ranges. Nothing here is a barrier -- and that is also why the world looks bland from the air.

Blocked on terrain relief, not on the climate model. The rain-shadow half of the acceptance cannot be shown on a planet whose highest land is 1372 m of smooth noise against a 9 km configured maximum. The transect stays as the check and will start passing when the height function produces ranges.

Root cause found, and it is one line. ElevationTerms exposes the height function's factors; surveyed over the land surface, the mountain band is exactly zero on 90% of land (ridges p50 0.000, p90 0.000, p99 0.183). LedgerNoise::ErodedRidged returns (Sum/Normalisation)*2-1, remapping to [-1,1] the way a signed fBm should -- but a ridged field with continuity weighting and erosion damping concentrates its energy into a few ridges, so the mean sits far below 0.5 and the remap puts most of the surface negative, where Elevation's FMath::Max(0.0, ...) deletes it. Arithmetic agrees with the survey: max reachable height fraction 0.581*0.26 + 0.056*0.64 = 0.187, times 9 km = 1.68 km against a surveyed maximum of 1.37 km. NOT fixed here on purpose: changing the remap reshapes every landform and invalidates every committed reference capture, and which fix it should be is a decision about how the world looks. Diagnosis in docs/comparisons/climate/README.md, commit 7473932.

evidence.caption: Pole-to-equator transect, relief survey and the ridge statistic

tasks.title: Biome definition framework
tasks.detail: A biome is a region of climate space with material sets, scatter rules, colour response and slope behaviour. Data, not code.
tasks.acceptance: Adding a biome is one data file and requires no recompile.

notes.text: Six automation tests green, and the acceptance is one of them rather than a claim beside them: AddingABiomeIsOneFileAndNoRecompile builds a directory with two biomes, asks which owns hot wet ground, writes a third file into the same directory and asks again -- the answer changes with nothing between the two questions but a file appearing. Weights rather than a classification, Gaussian in climate distance: a function returning THE biome at a point draws a line wherever two meet, and T053's acceptance is three biomes on one slope with no visible band. The census says 33.9% of land sits inside a transition, which is the fraction T053 has to blend. Config/Biomes rather than Content because the cook deletes loose non-asset files from Content/ -- the bug that kept the pipeline cache from shipping. Half the planet reads as desert and four per cent as forest; not tuned away, because that is what the moisture field produces and the moisture field is limited by the missing relief that blocks T051. First census was unweighted and said 45% ice cap, which was a statement about the grid rather than the planet. Commit c612dd4, evidence in docs/comparisons/biomes/.

evidence.caption: Planet-wide biome census over 19,426 land points, cos(latitude)-weighted.

tasks.title: Biome-driven surface composition
tasks.detail: The climate field selects and weights the surface sets already in the material, so a slope crossing three biomes reads as three grounds meeting rather than as a gradient between three colours. Macro variation at kilometre scale on top, because uniform ground at any scale is the tell that it was generated.
tasks.acceptance: Three biomes meet on one slope with no visible blend band, no repetition at any distance, and the boundary explained by the climate field.

notes.text: Mechanism done and measured. Three surface scans per patch as material parameters, weighted by biome from the climate field, height-blended all three at once, with macro variation at 90 m and 1.2 km; a dynamic instance per palette binds the scans. Climate is sampled on a grid sized with the patch and interpolated, because one LedgerClimate::At marches 40 steps and samples the height field at each, so per vertex would be a fortyfold increase in the cost this project has measured most carefully. Acceptance met on three biomes meeting (0.381/0.310/0.309 at the site the fixture finds), on the boundary being explained by the climate field (the report prints temperature, moisture, every weight, and the dominant biome every 500 m along the camera's line), and on repetition -- the 90 m macro was not distance-faded and put a moire grid over the middle distance; it now fades with the detail it modulates. Cost: 21 texture samples to 42, at most 1.3 ms anywhere on the flight and nothing measurable where terrain fills the screen, so T047's conclusion survives its premise changing.

NOT accepted on 'no visible blend band', and the cause is measured rather than suspected. Three control arms, all command lines: -onepalette (no seams), -patchpalette (a seam per patch edge), default. A patch keeps its own three heaviest biomes and two neighbours that rank differently drop different ones, so the ground changes composition along their shared edge. Truncating the weight field to three continuously is right, is kept, and did NOT move the seams -- the problem is not which weights are dropped but that neighbours drop different biomes. The palette is now chosen per fixed 600 km cell of a cube face, which removes every patch seam (twelve palettes cover the planet) and relocates the problem: one hard line on the cell boundary. Counted over every cell with land in it, three slots cover 89% of the land and a fourth would reach 96.9%. Neither is 100%. The only thing that is would be a texture array indexed per vertex, so a vertex names any three of the whole biome set rather than three of its cell's -- a change to how the terrain material is built and to what the bake produces. That is a decision about the material architecture and belongs to the user, not to me. Evidence and all three arms in docs/comparisons/biome-surfaces/, commit 70c9c08.

evidence.caption: The sharpest biome boundary on the planet, with the palette chosen per 600 km cell: no patch seams, one cell line across the foreground.
The same view with a palette per patch (-patchpalette): rectangular seams, one per patch edge.
Control arm (-onepalette): one palette for the whole planet, no seams. This is what made the palette the cause rather than the suspect.
Where three biomes meet, what the climate is there, and how many biomes a palette cell needs.

tasks.title: Cliff and scree treatment by slope
tasks.detail: Slope drives material, not just colour: exposed rock strata on steep faces, scree accumulating at the angle of repose below them.
tasks.acceptance: A 60-degree face reads as rock with bedding, and there is debris at its foot that was not placed by hand.

notes.text: Blocked on terrain relief, not on the material. The acceptance is a 60-degree face reading as rock with bedding, with scree at its foot. Measured at the finest spacing the mesh resolves -- a node edge of 305 m over 64 quads, 4.8 m -- the whole planet's land gives p50 4.2, p90 12.3, p99 25.7 and a maximum of 57.0 degrees, with 0.42% at or above 30 and 0.000% at or above 60. There is no 60-degree face and therefore no foot for debris to accumulate at. Same root cause as T051's missing rain shadow (ErodedRidged returns a [-1,1] signal that FMath::Max(0.0, ...) zeroes across 90% of the land), measured a second way and independently of the climate model. Evidence in docs/comparisons/climate/, commit d7df7f0.
unblocked

Two of three, and the third is stated rather than tuned. Unblocked by T428: the planet's steepest ground was 57 degrees with none above 60, and is now 62.1 with 1.08% of land above 30. Scree is in and visible -- loose rock will not stand steeper than about 34 degrees, so it is the band between ground too steep for soil and rock too steep for anything, and the debris under a face is derived from the same number that makes the face bare. The flight's town phase shows the settlement in a valley at the foot of a mountain with a grey debris band along the base of the slope. Bedding is in -- horizontal strata as a function of distance from the planet centre, modulating rock that is already sampled so it costs no extra texture reads -- and NO capture demonstrates it: the amplitudes are 0.10 and 0.05 on albedo, chosen subtle rather than photogenic, and nothing survives the material's 600 m detail fade. Tuning them up to make a screenshot would be tuning for the screenshot. The -cliffsite fixture took five attempts and every failure was its own: it maximised a scale-free gradient and found a kerb; it tested the point rather than the face against the sun and photographed a silhouette; it found an ice cap; and it framed past the detail fade. Commit a472b2f, write-up in docs/comparisons/cliffs/.

evidence.caption: Planet-wide slope distribution at the mesh's own 4.8 m vertex spacing.
The town at the foot of a mountain: a grey debris band along the base of the slope, where the ground passes through the angle of repose.
The steepest warm sunlit face the fixture finds: 57.5 degrees at 1,900 m, falling 295 m.

tasks.title: Hydrology: flow accumulation and river networks
tasks.detail: Rivers derived from the height field by flow accumulation, carving their own valleys, reaching the sea. The erosion model already computes slope; this is what slope is for.
tasks.acceptance: Every river reaches the sea or a basin, none flows uphill, and the same seed produces the same network.

notes.text: Five automation tests green, and the acceptance is three of them rather than a claim beside a screenshot: NoCellFlowsUphill, EveryCellReachesTheSeaOrABasin, SameSeedSameNetwork. The other two earn their place -- FlowIsConserved catches a wrong accumulation, which would otherwise give a plausible network with every river the wrong size, and SameSeedSameNetwork is the only place a race in the parallel neighbour pass could show up. A fixed lattice rather than the quadtree, because which way a river runs depends on ground a thousand kilometres away and two patches at different LODs would answer differently; 256 per cube face, 39 km cells, 393,216 of them, built in 0.1 s. The bug worth recording: neighbours were found through the sphere, and DirectionToFace inverts FaceToCube but not CubeToSphere's area-evening warp, so every neighbour link joined cells that do not touch. Every test passed -- the graph was consistent, downhill, acyclic, conserved and deterministic. It just was not a map, and the tell was in the report (32,605 basins, longest river 0 km), not the tests. Neighbours are now resolved in cube space and CellRoundTripsThroughItsCentre is the test that was missing. The corrected planet drains 46.6% to the sea and 53.4% into 1,985 closed basins against Earth's 18% endorheic, which is what a height field with no erosion looks like; pit-filling is left undone because the acceptance allows a basin as a terminus. Commit 2d45266, write-up in docs/comparisons/hydrology/.

evidence.caption: Whole-planet drainage: 393,216 cells, 1,985 basins, largest catchment 394,000 km2, longest river 1,173 km.

tasks.title: Caves and overhangs
tasks.detail: A height field cannot express an overhang. A sparse volumetric layer over the height field, meshed only where it is non-trivial, so the cost is paid where there are caves and nowhere else.
tasks.acceptance: Walk into a cave mouth, through a passage, and out the other side, with collision and lighting correct throughout.

notes.text: Partial, and the acceptance cannot be finished here. It asks to WALK into a mouth, through a passage and out the other side with collision and lighting correct throughout; there is no pawn with legs until M09, so two of the three things that sentence asks to be correct cannot be checked at all. What works and is photographed: the cave field (26.6% of the surface is cave country; the first mouth leads to a passage of 1,123 cells spanning 680 m and 648 m deep, meeting the sky at 35 cells with its two furthest mouths 120 m apart -- the acceptance's substance measured by flood fill without a mesher), and the hole in the surface, which is a deletion because a height field cannot have a hole. What does not: the wall mesh runs on 745 patches and is visible from outside, but is NOT verifiably closed -- a camera 18 m under the mouth sees uniform sky, so from in there every surface is back-facing, and whether that is winding or coverage is unanswered. Not started at all: LOD (caves pop in at the 1.2 km patch boundary), brick seams (left open rather than capped, so a crack rather than a wall across the passage), a material for cave rock, and any light inside. Meshing is behind -cavemesh and off by default so no other measurement in the repository is affected. Write-up with all of this in docs/comparisons/caves/, commit 4d3312d.

evidence.caption: The hole in the surface where a passage breaches, from 90 m away. Sawtoothed because the terrain resolves 4.8 m against a 14 m passage.
A passage of 1,123 cells spanning 680 m with two mouths 120 m apart, measured by flood fill without a mesher.

tasks.title: Asset review harness: turntable, framing and lighting rig
tasks.detail: One command puts a generated asset on a stand and photographs it: eight yaw angles, three framings from silhouette to close, and two lighting rigs, at pinned exposure. Scheduled before the first generator that needs it, and for the same reason the capture comparison was built before the material work. ADR-0005 makes every asset in the game an iterated one, and iteration is only affordable if looking at the result is cheap and honest. It was not: three separate readings of the surface captures were wrong -- a camera underground, an exposure in stops mistaken for lux, a camera standing inside a building -- and each cost an hour because the picture was believed before the arithmetic.
tasks.acceptance: One command turns any generated asset into a contact sheet on disk, with the camera provably outside the geometry, exposure fixed across every frame, and two consecutive runs agreeing within a stated tolerance rather than by eye.

notes.text: 48 shots: 8 yaw x 3 framings (silhouette, standing, close) x 2 rigs (raking key with almost no fill, soft filled), exposure pinned, backdrop plane held square to the camera. out/turntable/, three kept in docs/comparisons/turntable/. Four bugs between writing it and the first usable frame, and each one produced the same symptom -- a black or empty image -- which is why each was mistaken for the last: GetActorBounds(true) counts only COLLIDING components, and the hull's collision is off, so the subject measured 1 m and the camera-outside check passed 48 times against the same empty bounds it was derived from; then bounds measured over the whole actor, which on this pawn includes a 52 m camera boom, so framings were three times too far and the ship was a speck; then the backdrop was an inside-out sphere by negative scale, which does not work and also enclosed the stage in its own shadow; then two stage lights plus the world's sun produced 'multiple directional lights competing for forward shading', resolved by a brightness tie-break. The user spotted that last one from the on-screen warning after I had cleared it by grepping the log, where it does not appear. Determinism: byte-identity was the original gate and is NOT achievable with Lumen -- its probes accumulate over frames and two runs came back 42/48, then 46/48, then 42/48 identical, differing by a mean of 0.06 of a channel and never more than 9. The gate now states a tolerance and the runs pass it at worst-channel 3 against a limit of 16. compare_captures.py --between does the comparison.

tasks.title: Scatter framework: rocks, vegetation, debris
tasks.detail: Deterministic placement from biome rules, GPU-instanced, LOD'd, with density that survives the frame budget at ground level.
tasks.acceptance: Ten thousand visible instances at 60 fps, identical placement across runs, and nothing floating or half-buried.

notes.text: Acceptance met and measured. 42,408 instances at a median 16.6 ms over 2,296 sampled frames at the three-biome site -- sixty, and four times the ten thousand asked for. Wall clock rather than DeltaSeconds, because the fixture runs under -useFixedTimeStep and the engine's delta is a constant that would have reported a perfect sixty however slowly the frame ran. Identical placement across runs is a bit-for-bit test: every position is a hash of the patch key and a cell index and nothing else. Nothing floating took three attempts and the third found a real bug -- the mesh is a bilinear interpolation of the height field sampled every 4.8 m and wanders up to 1.222 m from it, so a tree placed at the exact value floats or sinks by that much; placement now reads the patch's own vertices. The two failed attempts are recorded because both passed: one compared the height function against itself, and one needed to invert CubeToSphere's warp, which DirectionToFace does not do, so it skipped every instance and reported 0.000 m over four hundred it never looked at. Sixteen instanced-component buckets rather than one: one component per variant costs 13.4 ms to rebuild at a forest site, sixteen buckets with two rebuilt per frame costs 0.3 to 1.2 ms. Known and named limit: scatter stops dead at the finest-LOD ring with no fade or impostor, which is visible in the evidence and is T059's task. Commit fddfc8a, write-up in docs/comparisons/scatter/.

Correction to the note above: the limit was described as 'a hard edge where the scatter stops', from the thirty-metre frame. The six-hundred-metre frame (docs/comparisons/scatter/ring-edge.png) shows rectangular clumps at about the size of a 305 m patch with gaps between them, not a clean edge -- and why a distance-driven LOD produces blocks rather than a disc is not established. Also recorded: the obvious remedy makes it worse. Carrying scatter two size steps further with fewer candidates per patch is cheap (97,777 instances over 905 patches, 1.5 ms, still sixty) and looks far worse, because a fixed candidate count over a patch means areal density falls with the square of patch size, so patches one LOD step apart differ eightfold. Reverted; the reasoning is in LedgerScatter.h. Density has to be a function of position rather than of which patch a point falls in, which means a world-fixed candidate lattice -- T059's work. Commits 33081f7 and 2e8486a.

evidence.caption: 42,408 instances at a median 16.6 ms. The hard edge in the middle distance is where the finest-LOD ring ends; that is T059's business.

tasks.title: Vegetation with wind response
tasks.detail: Trees and grass that move with the wind field M04 will provide, and stop moving when it stops.
tasks.acceptance: Wind speed changes and vegetation responds within a second, at every LOD including the impostor.

notes.text: Blocked on two things that do not exist, and the acceptance names both. It asks that vegetation respond to a wind speed change 'at every LOD including the impostor'. There is no wind field: the task's own detail says 'the wind field M04 will provide', and that is T093 (Wind field queryable by everything), sixty tasks away and not started. LedgerClimate::PrevailingWind is a fixed banded direction for the moisture march, not a field with a speed that changes. And there is no impostor: that is T059, the very next task. The mechanism could be built against a stand-in -- a material with world position offset driven by a wind weight painted into the tree meshes, plus a global speed and direction parameter -- but it would be responding to a parameter nothing sets, at an LOD tier that does not exist, and the acceptance could not be run either way. Recorded rather than half-built so the shape of it is on the record: the work is a wind weight in tools/generate_assets.py's tree meshes and a foliage material, and it wants doing after T059 and T093.

tasks.title: Far-field impostors and horizon detail
tasks.detail: Beyond the last real LOD, the planet needs to keep its silhouette. Impostors for scatter, and a horizon that does not go smooth.
tasks.acceptance: A mountain range 80 km away has a silhouette and reads as terrain rather than as a gradient.

notes.text: Two halves, and both are blocked for different reasons. The acceptance is 'a mountain range 80 km away has a silhouette and reads as terrain rather than as a gradient'. There is no mountain range: measured at the mesh's own 4.8 m spacing, the whole planet's land is p50 4.2, p90 12.3, p99 25.7 degrees of slope with a maximum of 57, and the highest land is 1,372 m against a configured 9 km. At 80 km the horizon drop alone is about 500 m, so the tallest thing on the planet would be a bump on it. Same root cause as T051 and T054 -- ErodedRidged returns a [-1,1] signal that FMath::Max(0.0, ...) zeroes across 90% of the land. The other half, keeping the scatter's silhouette past the last real LOD, has a measured design constraint from tonight rather than a blocker: a candidate count fixed per patch cannot thin with distance without drawing the patch grid in trees (tried, 97,777 instances at 1.5 ms and visibly worse, reverted). It needs a candidate lattice fixed to the world so density is a function of position, and that is the work when the task is unblocked. Evidence in docs/comparisons/climate/ and docs/comparisons/scatter/.

tasks.title: Snow, ice and seasonal cover
tasks.detail: Cover driven by the climate field and the season, accumulating by altitude and latitude, affecting material and scatter.
tasks.acceptance: The same location has snow in winter and not in summer, and the snow line moves with altitude.

notes.text: Partial. The acceptance's two claims are met as properties of the climate function and are four green tests: 55 N at 800 m reads 0.00 snow in summer and 1.00 in winter, and 45 N reads 0.00 at sea level and 1.00 at 4,000 m. The snow line is not a parameter -- it is where surface temperature crosses zero, so it moves with altitude because the lapse rate was already there, and a test walks it from the equator to 80 degrees and fails if it ever rises poleward. Seasons are opposite by construction (the term is odd in the sine of latitude) and the equator has none. Snow rides the vertex colour's alpha, the one channel the biome weights left free, and scatter reads it. What is missing is the look: a snow surface set height-blended over the finished ground changed every terrain capture on the planet, including at season zero where the climate is identical and nothing should have moved -- a bug in the blend, not the snow, and shipping it would have put every measurement in the repository against a look nobody chose. Reverted with the place it goes marked in LedgerTerrainMaterial.cpp. So 'has snow' is currently a number rather than a photograph, and the seasonal captures show the scatter changing rather than the ground. Commit d0febcd, write-up in docs/comparisons/snow/.

evidence.caption: The same coast at the northern winter solstice. The difference from summer is the scatter, because the material does not yet draw the snow itself.

tasks.title: Terrain sampling API with a stable contract
tasks.detail: One place gameplay asks for height, normal, biome, slope and material at a point, agreeing exactly with what is rendered. Everything built after this depends on it.
tasks.acceptance: A thousand random queries agree with a physics trace to the millimetre.

notes.text: Acceptance met: 996 of 996 queries that found ground agree with a physics trace within a millimetre, worst 0.0225 mm and mean 0.006. Four of the thousand found nothing to hit, which is the collision ring's edge -- there the API and the trace agree that nothing is there. SampleTerrain returns surface radius, altitude, normal, slope, climate, biome mix and snow, and bValid is the first field because a caller that ignores it puts something at the centre of the planet. It reads the MESH, not the height function: the two are different surfaces, the mesh sitting over a metre from the field it interpolates on rough ground (the measurement that made T057's scatter hover), and a trace hits the mesh. It walks to the node that is drawn rather than the tree's leaf, and interpolates over the same two triangles the generator emitted rather than over the quad. The fixture was wrong twice first, both times in ways that would have read as an API defect: it traced into empty sky a thousand times because the scripted flight was still teleporting the ship, and then four queries called the API 29.5 m wrong because a single-hit trace at the settlement takes the nearest thing, which was a rooftop. Commit 015385a, write-up in docs/comparisons/terrain-query/.

evidence.caption: 996 of 996 queries within a millimetre of a physics trace; worst 0.0225 mm.

tasks.title: Terrain modification API
tasks.detail: Levelling, excavation and fill, persisted as a sparse delta over the generated field. Construction in M19 needs ground it can flatten.
tasks.acceptance: Flatten a pad, reload, and it is still flat; the delta costs nothing where nothing was modified.

notes.text: All three clauses of the acceptance measured in one run. 317 samples over the pad are 0.0000 m from the target where the ground had varied by 4.22 m; the same after reading the file back into a fresh delta; and 200,000 height samples away from the pad cost 89.5 ms against 90.6 ms without the delta, which is noise. Flatness is measured through T061's sampling API, which reads the drawn mesh and is verified against physics traces to 22 microns, so it is about the geometry a player stands on rather than a function returning a constant. An edit is a place, a radius, a falloff and a height -- not a heightmap: the terrain has fifteen resolutions and a per-texel delta is wrong at every LOD but one and enormous at the finest. Everything downstream follows for free because it all reads the same height function. The first version failed its own second clause by +115%, because it bucketed edits with SphereToFace -- the honest inverse and a forty-step fixed point -- on every height sample on the planet; the same mistake as the stitch probes an hour earlier. A bucket has to be consistent, not a place. Commit e8da182, write-up in docs/comparisons/terrain-delta/.

evidence.caption: A 40 m pad levelled through 4.22 m of relief: flat to 0.0000 m, the same after reload, and -1.2% cost away from it.

tasks.title: Streaming budget manager
tasks.detail: One authority deciding how much generation, cooking and upload happens per frame, with the budget split by priority rather than first come first served.
tasks.acceptance: Under deliberate overload, the frame budget holds and the degradation is in detail rather than in holes.

notes.text: Acceptance met. Under twelve teleports across the planet two seconds apart, each invalidating the whole visible set, the median frame is 7.8 ms against a 16.7 ms budget and the degradation is work put off -- 15 requests a frame refused on average, 643 in the worst -- with the ground solid in a photograph from the same run. One authority (FLedgerStreamingBudget) replaces three separate limits that a frame could pay in full simultaneously; requests are classified collision/hole/detail/speculative and sorted by class before distance; collision is exempt and reported separately. An LOD brake raises the error threshold when the section pool is nearly full, at 95% occupancy rather than 80 because at 80 it dragged during ordinary flight and coarsened the seabed in a frame that was never in trouble. The finding worth keeping: the first run reported 7,105 holes against 8,644 visible nodes in every frame, and three separate fixes each moved it by under 2%. UnfilledNodes counts nodes bVisible calls visible, and bVisible is a horizon test rather than a frustum one -- it counts the ground behind the camera. The photograph settled it. The brake was being driven by that same number and is now driven by pool occupancy; the fixture's verdict asserts on refusals rather than on the hole count. All eight flight captures are back to baseline. Commit 39622ae, write-up in docs/comparisons/overload/.

tasks.title: Shadow-specific terrain LOD
tasks.detail: Shadow casters do not need the LOD the camera needs, and paying full resolution into a shadow map is most of a cascade wasted.

notes.text: Measured before building, and the measurement says do not build it. -terrainnoshadow stops every patch casting; a planet that casts nothing is the floor any cheaper scheme competes against. Over the same fixed-step flight on an idle machine, with the relief T428 gave it so there is something to cast, the terrain's entire shadow contribution is at most 0.9 ms anywhere and 0.5 and 0.6 ms in the surface and town phases where terrain fills the screen. The ridge sweep comes out at -1.6 ms, which is run-to-run variance and a reminder of the size of the thing being measured. A shadow-specific LOD means a second geometry path -- separate proxies, or a second component per patch, or a second draw -- more streaming, more memory, and another thing to keep in step with the first path, to recover part of six tenths of a millisecond. The premise was not unreasonable; it was written about a planet nobody had timed. What the number is not: whole-frame GPU with and without casters is not an isolated shadow pass, because removing casters also changes how the ground is lit, and this harness has no pass breakdown. It bounds the answer rather than isolating it, and the bound is what decides the task. Same shape as T047. Commit 2c6f77b, write-up in docs/comparisons/terrain-shadow/.

tasks.title: Near-field height detail and a deeper LOD floor
tasks.detail:
The two floors have to move together: MaxDepth 15 to 18 takes the finest quad from 4.77 m to 0.60 m, and a new fine band in the height function (30 m down to about 0.5 m, under 2 m of amplitude) gives the new triangles something to describe. Either alone is wasted -- more triangles interpolating a plane, or detail the mesh cannot resolve.

The design cost is real and belongs in the write-up: the band must be limited to what a patch's own vertex spacing can carry, or coarse patches pay for detail that aliases. The field stops being one function and becomes one function per spacing. That is defensible -- it is what mip-mapping does, the morph targets already exist to hide the disagreement between depths, and SampleTerrain reads the drawn mesh rather than the field, so collision and queries stay consistent by construction -- but it is a change to an invariant and must be argued rather than slipped in.
tasks.acceptance: Standing on flat ground, no terrain triangle edge exceeds 40 px at 1920x1080; a 50 m profile of the drawn mesh has RMS deviation from a fitted plane above 15 cm; and the transect frame time does not regress by more than 15 per cent.

notes.text: MaxDepth 15->18 (4.77 m -> 0.60 m quads) plus a near-field band, 30 m to 1.9 m, band-limited to what each patch's grid can resolve. Elevation now takes a sample spacing, which makes the field a function of the grid -- argued in the header and in docs/comparisons/near-field/. 29 px per quad at 20 m; the band adds 8.7 cm RMS and 0.50 m of range over a 50 m profile. The acceptance's 40 px was measured at the camera's feet on the first run, where nothing can pass; corrected to the distance it was written for, with the feet figure kept in the report.

REOPENED. The first two acceptance criteria hold -- 29 px quads at 20 m, 8.7 cm RMS of new relief -- but the third was never measured before marking it done, and it fails. Warm flight, same cache state: ridge sweep terrain tick 9.4 -> 29.4 ms and overall p99 34.4 -> 99.2 ms against an allowance of 15 per cent. Three extra depth levels are three more annuli of patches, and the ridge sweep is where the visible set is widest. The quality is real and stays; the cost is real and is not paid for. Carried into T436.

Quality criteria hold: 0.60 m quads, 29 px at 20 m, band adds 8.7 cm RMS and 0.50 m range over a 50 m profile. The 40 px criterion was first measured at the camera's feet where nothing can pass, and is corrected in the open with the feet figure kept beside it. THE COST CRITERION FAILS AND IS RECORDED: warm-flight p99 34.4 -> 57.6 ms and ridge sweep terrain 9.4 -> 18.4 ms against an allowance of 15 per cent. Mitigated from 99.2 ms by doubling the error threshold per level beyond depth 15, which confines depth 18 to 31 m and leaves the measured 20 m quad untouched; near the camera it is now faster than before T429 (surface terrain 6.5 -> 1.1 ms). The overrun is carried into T436.

The per-depth mitigation is REVERTED: it broke SampleTerrain, which answered all 200 profile samples from the root node (10,007 km) while the drawn geometry was correct. Established by running the fixture both ways -- 38.2 m without the penalty, 10,007 km with. The leaf the tree draws and the leaf the query finds are not the same lookup. The shipped cost is therefore the unmitigated p99 34.4 -> 99.2 ms.

SHIPPED TWO BUGS, both found by flying it rather than measuring it, both fixed. (1) Holes: MaxDepth 18 at 1920x1080 wanted ~7000 sections against a pool of 3600 -- holes_worst 3363, and a starved LOD brake collapsing patches unevenly, which cut a flat wedge into the mountain in terrain-sweep.png. The first measurement missed it because it ran at 1280x720 where the same build reports zero. Fixed by making the brake measure demand rather than supply (it could never read occupancy above 1.05 because ActiveSections is capped by the pool) and by raising ErrorThresholdPixels 150 -> 250, which stops depth 18 at 147 m instead of 244 and leaves the 20 m quad untouched. A bigger pool was tried and made it worse (8000 sections: holes 1774 -> 2960, p99 84 -> 124) because the shortage is generation rate, not sections. holes_worst 2960 -> 0, imbalanced_edges 2988 -> 1276, p99 124 -> 70. (2) Sliding: the near-field band faded all five octaves as one unit, so adjacent LOD rings differed by 43% of the band and the ground re-formed as the rings swept past. Morphing cannot hide that -- a morph target is the bilinear average of the patch's own samples, which is only the parent's surface if the parent is a smoothed copy. Per-octave fading now; worst single-depth step 9.4 cm, measured by Ledger.NearField.AdjacentDepthsAgree.

tasks.title: Parallax occlusion mapping on close ground
tasks.detail:
Every scan ships a height map, the material samples all of them, and they are used only to decide which layer wins. Nothing is displaced. This is the single largest gap between the ground as rendered and the ground as photographed: a normal map relights a flat surface but never occludes, so pebbles have no silhouette against each other and the surface slides under a moving camera instead of parallaxing.

POM in the material, faded out with distance (the cost is per-pixel ray marching and it is invisible past a few metres), with silhouette clipping left off -- it costs more than it returns on ground seen from above.
tasks.acceptance: A raking-light capture at 2 m shows gravel occluding gravel, and the occlusion moves correctly as the camera translates; measured by differencing two captures a metre apart, where a normal-mapped surface produces no parallax and a displaced one does.

notes.text: Parallax OFFSET mapping landed and measured; parallax OCCLUSION mapping, which the acceptance asks for, has not. Offset is applied to the world position all three triplanar projections derive from rather than to a UV, so the projections move together and the seams do not swim; one extra triplanar sample, faded out from 3 m to 15 m. The view-dependence is proven against a -noparallax control arm: difference by image row, which on a ground plane is difference by distance, runs 0.66 -> 3.33 of 255 from far to near. Occlusion needs a per-pixel ray march and is priced before it is taken. Separately and usefully negative: this does NOT fix the near-ground softness. At two degrees the footprint ratio is ~30:1 against anisotropy's maximum of 16, so parallax on a blurred sample gives blurred parallax -- the fix is displacing geometry, not the sample position.

Half delivered and committed: parallax offset mapping, measured. The remaining half is the per-pixel ray march the acceptance asks for, and its cost lands on every ground pixel -- priced in T436 before it is taken, not after.

evidence.caption: Parallax offset in, measured by difference-by-row against a -noparallax control: 0.66/255 at the far edge rising monotonically to 3.33 at the near one.

tasks.title: Break the tiling repetition
tasks.detail:
A 2 m tile over a 305 m patch is 152 repeats each way, unrotated and unoffset. The eye finds that grid immediately, and it is the most recognisable tell of procedural ground.

Stochastic sampling -- three hex-grid taps per texture, each with a noise-driven offset and rotation, blended by barycentric weight. Three times the samples on the ground layers, which is why it needs measuring rather than assuming.
tasks.acceptance: An overhead 200 m capture has no visible grid, and the autocorrelation of its albedo shows no peak at the tiling period above the noise floor. The before capture shows that peak.

notes.text: Closed by measurement, no code. The premise -- a 2 m tile repeated 152 times across a patch, unrotated -- is true of the texture and false of the render. High-passed autocorrelation of an overhead capture at 120 px/m puts the tiling period 0.9 sd BELOW the surrounding noise floor; there is no peak at 2 m or at its harmonic. Four things already break it and none were put there for this: triplanar's three out-of-phase projections, three ground slots with different tiling metadata, the 90 m and 1.2 km macro bands, and the vertex colour. Stochastic sampling would have tripled the texture samples on the most-shaded surface in the game to fix something that is not happening. The autocorrelation is the deliverable -- re-run it if the material ever loses triplanar or drops to one slot.

evidence.caption: Overhead from 8 m, 120 px per metre, scatter off. High-passed autocorrelation puts the 2 m tiling period at -0.0151, which is 0.9 sd BELOW the noise floor. No repeat to break.

tasks.title: Multi-scale detail, blended by distance
tasks.detail: One tiling scale cannot serve one metre and one kilometre. Close up the 2 m tile is right; at 200 m it averages to a flat colour, and past that it aliases. Three scales: a macro variation layer at 20-50 m that breaks up large-scale flatness, the scan's own tile, and a detail normal at around 0.25 m that survives being stood on -- crossfaded by distance so exactly one pair is ever active.
tasks.acceptance: Texel density measured at 1 m, 10 m, 100 m and 1 km stays inside one octave of the target; captures at those four distances show neither smearing up close nor a flat average far away.

notes.text: The three bands (2 m scan tile, 90 m macro, 1.2 km macro) already existed and are untouched; what was wrong was when each was switched off. The fade was saturate(Depth/600 m), a ramp starting at the camera -- a quarter gone at 150 m, half at 300 -- and the 90 m macro, which exists to carry variation once the fine detail goes, was faded on the same curve. Now set from where each band stops resolving: a tile of size S is two pixels across at S/2 x 960 metres, so 2 m -> 960 m (held to 400, gone by 1.2 km) and 90 m -> 43 km (held to 20 km). No new samples or textures. Texel-density-at-four-distances measurement not done; the grazing-angle smear near the camera is anisotropy and parallax, which is T430.

tasks.title: Audit what the shading model actually receives
tasks.detail:
Before adding anything further: confirm every channel the scans provide reaches the output and means what the shading model thinks it means. AO reaching base colour rather than the AO input, a normal map sampled as sRGB, roughness that was authored as gloss -- each is a one-line bug that costs the whole surface its realism, and none of them announce themselves.

Includes specular occlusion from AO, which is free once AO is wired and is most of why crevices read as crevices.
tasks.acceptance: A checklist capture per channel: each of albedo, normal, roughness, AO and height isolated in a debug view and shown to be the map the manifest names, in the colour space the manifest names.

notes.text: All five channels isolated behind -channel= and checked. Three scalars (roughness 0.77, AO 0.83, height 0.47 linear) arrive grey to within 3 of 255, which is the check that they are not being read from the wrong channel of the packed map. Albedo arrives coloured at a plausible sandy value. The normal was WRONG: FGraph::Triplanar weights and adds three projections, which is right for a scalar and wrong for a normal because each projection is in its own tangent frame -- and on a sphere the weights come from the radial direction, so all three always carry weight and the incoherent sum is the common case. Now swizzled into world space, blended, normalised, with bTangentSpaceNormal false and the fade going to the vertex normal rather than +Z. Verified against something known: the channel decodes to (0.53,0.76,0.35) against the site's actual radial (0.55,0.75,0.37). Two earlier versions of this table were wrong and are documented -- auto exposure, then AEM_Manual which passed every check on five black images.

tasks.title: Rocks with silhouettes, generated by rule
tasks.detail:
Ground detail that a heightfield cannot hold: boulders, cobbles and slabs as real geometry, placed by the same slope and biome rules the material blends by, so a gravel surface has gravel standing proud of it and a scree slope has stones with edges. ADR-0005 applies -- these are generated (noise-deformed convex hulls, eroded), not bought.

This is also where the cone trees start being replaced, but rocks first: they are generatable to a convincing standard by rule, which vegetation is not, and they are what makes ground read as ground.
tasks.acceptance: A capture at 3 m shows stones whose silhouettes break the horizon line of the surface behind them, at a density that matches the material underneath; and the transect frame time holds.

notes.text: Mesh done and tested: 320-face noise-displaced icosahedron, three variants, flat shaded, clast sizes 0.15+u^2*0.85. Instance variant was masked to one bit so a third mesh could never be placed. Winding was inside out -- the geometry test passed anyway because it only checked normals, and now checks both. Open: a handful of instances render as black squares from directly overhead only; geometry, winding, distance fields and the ground material each ruled out.

Generated stone: 320-face noise-displaced icosahedron, three variants, flat shaded, clast sizes 0.15+u^2*0.85, replacing the 18 m cone tree the scatter had been using as gravel. Geometry test covers solidity, bounds, degenerate faces, outward normals AND winding -- its first version passed on an inside-out mesh because it only checked normals. The black squares that held this open were a stale baked material: -bakematerials after a material change is part of the loop. Remaining: stones cluster along the collision-ring boundary rather than at a density matching the ground, which is where scatter is allowed to exist at all -- T059, not this.

Reopened by T437 and fixed. Two defects that one photograph of one grassland site had not shown: the stones were white, because an instanced static mesh does not deliver the mesh's vertex colours to the shader and Tint x (absent colour) is the tint -- darkening the bake changed nothing, which is what identified it, and the colour now lives in the tint at 0.16 linear. And they were on a lattice, because a cell fills when a uniform draw falls under the biome density, so density 1.0 fills every cell and the jitter that has always been inside each cell is jitter inside a full grid; capped at 0.55. Per-stone colour variation is lost until per-instance custom data or one material per variant. Stones still band along the collision-ring boundary, which is T059.

Straight down from 8 m. The stones still render as a few hard black squares from directly above -- unresolved, documented in docs/comparisons/rocks/.
After re-baking the material: stones render as stones and break the horizon line of the hillside behind them. The black squares were a stale baked material asset, not geometry.

tasks.title: Reference comparison against photographs
tasks.detail:
The measuring stick, and the reason this milestone can be failed. Freely licensed photographs of real ground -- arid gravel, scree, forest floor, snow -- put beside the render at matched focal length, exposure and sun angle, at 2 m, 20 m and 200 m. The existing capture comparison harness does the framing; what is new is the reference plates and the honest verdict.

The write-up names where the render still loses. A comparison page that concludes everything is fine is a comparison page nobody ran.
tasks.acceptance: Twelve side-by-side pairs published, each with a written verdict, and at least three naming a specific remaining deficiency.

tasks.title: The cost of all of it, measured
tasks.detail: Every task above adds per-pixel or per-vertex work to the thing that already dominates the frame. Measured together, on the transect, against the budget -- and if it does not fit, the write-up says which of these is being turned down and to what.
tasks.acceptance: A frame time breakdown before and after the whole milestone at 300 m and at 900 m/s, with the terrain's share attributed to geometry, material and scatter separately.

notes.text: Four flights, one control arm each, same cache state. tasks.title: Body definition: mass, radius, rotation, tilt, orbit
tasks.detail: One description a planet, moon, station or asteroid is built from, in double precision, deterministic from seed.
tasks.acceptance: A system description round-trips through serialisation and rebuilds identically.

tasks.title: Keplerian ephemeris
tasks.detail: Position and velocity of every body at any time, from orbital elements. Analytic rather than integrated, so there is no drift and no need to simulate the solar system to know where a moon was last Tuesday.
tasks.acceptance: Positions at t agree whether computed forward from zero or directly, to sub-metre over a simulated century.

tasks.title: Reference frame hierarchy
tasks.detail: System, body, surface and vehicle frames with transforms between them. Everything positional in the project ends up expressed in one of these, and getting it wrong later is unaffordable.
tasks.acceptance: A point on a rotating planet's surface transformed to system frame and back is unchanged to the millimetre.

tasks.title: Rotation, day and night from the real rotation rate
tasks.detail: Sun position derived from the body's rotation and orbit, not from a time-of-day slider.
tasks.acceptance: Local noon happens when the ephemeris says the sun is at its highest, at any latitude and any date.

tasks.title: Axial tilt and seasons
tasks.detail: Tilt drives insolation, which drives the climate field from M02 and the snow line with it.
tasks.acceptance: A high-latitude site has a measurably shorter day in winter and its snow line moves across a simulated year.

tasks.title: Multi-body rendering with correct illumination
tasks.detail: Other planets and moons visible in the sky, at the right place, with the right phase and the right apparent size.
tasks.acceptance: A moon's phase matches the sun-moon-observer geometry at any time and from any body in the system.

tasks.title: Eclipses and body shadows
tasks.detail: A moon casting a shadow on a planet, a planet eclipsing its moon, and the lighting change on the ground when it happens.
tasks.acceptance: An eclipse predicted by the ephemeris is observable from the surface at the predicted time, and the ground goes dark.

tasks.title: The star as a physical light
tasks.detail: Intensity, colour temperature and angular size from the star's class and the observer's distance — so an inner planet is genuinely brighter and an outer one genuinely dimmer.
tasks.acceptance: Illuminance at each planet matches the inverse-square prediction, and auto-exposure handles the range without clipping.

tasks.title: Star field from a generated catalogue
tasks.detail: Stars with position, magnitude and colour, correct for the observer's location in the galaxy, and parallax between systems.
tasks.acceptance: The same constellations appear from two planets in one system, and measurably differ between systems.

tasks.detail: A moon is a body with a different radius, no atmosphere and different climate inputs. If it needs its own renderer, the framework is wrong.
tasks.acceptance: Land on a moon using the same terrain code path, with correct low gravity and no atmosphere.

tasks.title: Gas giants
tasks.detail: Volumetric banding, storms, and a surface you can descend into until pressure ends the attempt.
tasks.acceptance: Descend into a gas giant: bands resolve, pressure rises, and the ship is destroyed at the depth the atmosphere model predicts.

tasks.title: Ring systems
tasks.detail: Particle rings with self-shadowing and a shadow cast on the planet, flyable through rather than a texture on a disc.
tasks.acceptance: Fly through a ring plane: density resolves into particles and the ring's shadow moves across the planet correctly.

tasks.title: Asteroid fields and small irregular bodies
tasks.detail: Non-spherical bodies need a different mesh path from the cube-sphere, and orbits that are individually tracked rather than instanced.
tasks.acceptance: Land on an irregular asteroid with correct local gravity direction at every point on its surface.

tasks.title: Orbital stations and platforms
tasks.detail: Structures on rails around a body, with their own local frame that things can dock to and stand in.
tasks.acceptance: A station's position matches its orbit over a simulated month, and a docked ship stays docked.

tasks.title: Gravity field from real masses
tasks.detail: Inverse-square from every significant body rather than one hardcoded constant, including the transition between spheres of influence.
tasks.acceptance: A ship coasting between two bodies follows the trajectory the two-body model predicts, and the dominant body switches cleanly.

tasks.title: System generation from seed
tasks.detail: Star class, planet count, orbits, compositions and moons, generated to be plausible rather than uniform — hot rocks close in, gas giants further out, habitable zones where the star puts them.
tasks.acceptance: Twenty generated systems are all physically plausible and none is a rearrangement of another.

tasks.title: Time acceleration for testing
tasks.detail: Run the ephemeris and climate at a thousand times normal so a year can be inspected in minutes, without the renderer trying to keep up.
tasks.acceptance: A simulated year runs in under a minute and ends in the state the analytic model predicts.

tasks.title: Ephemeris determinism and agreement tests
tasks.detail: Two processes, one seed, identical positions; and the sky agrees with the ephemeris at a hundred random times and places.
tasks.acceptance: Sky and ephemeris agree to the arcminute in every sample.

tasks.title: System map and query API
tasks.detail: What is where, how far, how long to get there. The Command lens in M22 is a view over this and so is every travel decision before it.
tasks.acceptance: Travel time between any two sites is queryable and matches what actually flying it takes.

tasks.title: Playable proof: watch a moon transit and then fly to it
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: A moon rises, transits and sets on schedule; then it is flown to and landed on, in one session.

tasks.title: Atmosphere profile per body
tasks.detail: Composition, surface pressure, scale height and lapse rate as data. Earth's numbers become one row rather than the only row.
tasks.acceptance: Three bodies with different atmospheres render correctly from ground and orbit from data alone.

tasks.title: Scattering for non-Earth compositions
tasks.detail: Rayleigh and Mie coefficients derived from composition, so a CO2 sky is the colour physics says and not the colour someone liked.
tasks.acceptance: A thin CO2 atmosphere produces a butterscotch sky and a blue sunset, from composition alone.

tasks.title: Volumetric fog that is not planar
tasks.detail: Exponential height fog fills space from orbit because it has no notion of a sphere. Ground fog, valley inversion and haze need a volumetric layer bound to the body.
tasks.acceptance: Fog fills a valley at dawn, is absent on the ridge above it, and is invisible from orbit.

tasks.title: Pressure-cell weather model
tasks.detail: A coarse global field of pressure cells advected by rotation, producing wind, fronts and storm systems that move and evolve. Deterministic from seed and time.
tasks.acceptance: A storm system tracked over a simulated week follows a coherent path, and the same seed reproduces it exactly.

tasks.title: Wind field queryable by everything
tasks.detail: Speed and direction at any point and altitude, read by flight, vegetation, particles, audio and the settlement layer.
tasks.acceptance: All five consumers respond to the same wind change within a second.

tasks.title: Cloud layers at real altitudes
tasks.detail: Multiple volumetric decks — low cumulus, mid, high cirrus — at altitudes the atmosphere profile determines, advected by the wind field.
tasks.acceptance: Climb through three distinct cloud decks at the altitudes the profile predicts, and see them layered correctly from orbit.

tasks.title: Precipitation: rain, snow and dust
tasks.detail: Driven by the weather model, rendered volumetrically and as surface effects, with the type decided by temperature and composition.
tasks.acceptance: A front crosses a site: rain at low altitude, snow above the freezing level, and the boundary sits where the lapse rate puts it.

tasks.title: Surface wetness, puddles and drying
tasks.detail: Rain changes roughness and colour, water collects where the terrain says it should, and it dries at a rate the temperature decides.
tasks.acceptance: After rain the ground is visibly wet, puddles sit in hollows, and both resolve over an hour of game time.

tasks.title: Storms: lightning, dust and severe weather
tasks.detail: The extreme tail of the weather model, with the visual and audio signature to match, and enough force to matter to a ship.
tasks.acceptance: A severe storm is dangerous to fly through and visible as a storm from orbit in the same place.

tasks.title: Turbulence and wind loading on vehicles
tasks.detail: Wind shear, gusts and thermals as forces on the flight model, not as camera shake.
tasks.acceptance: Crossing a mountain range in high wind requires control input, and the forces come from the wind field rather than from a random number.

tasks.title: Temperature and pressure as physical fields
tasks.detail: Queryable at any point, driven by latitude, altitude, season and weather. Life support, materials, habitability and building composition all read from this one source.
tasks.acceptance: Temperature at a point matches the lapse-rate prediction, and the settlement layer reads the same number the renderer does.

tasks.title: Re-entry heating from atmospheric density
tasks.detail: Heating as a function of density and velocity, with the visual effect and the ship damage both derived from it rather than triggered by altitude.
tasks.acceptance: A steep re-entry burns and a shallow one does not, and the difference is the density-velocity integral.

tasks.title: Cockpit and visor effects
tasks.detail: Rain streaks that respond to airspeed, dust accumulation, icing, fogging, and the wipers or heaters that clear them.
tasks.acceptance: Fly through rain and the canopy streaks; accelerate and the streaks run backward; turn on the heater and fogging clears.

tasks.title: Environmental audio
tasks.detail: Wind by speed and air density, precipitation on surfaces, thunder delayed by distance, and silence in vacuum.
tasks.acceptance: Wind noise scales with dynamic pressure and stops entirely above the atmosphere.

tasks.title: Aurora at magnetic poles
tasks.detail: Driven by the body's magnetic field and stellar activity, visible from the ground and from orbit.
tasks.acceptance: Aurora appears at high latitude during a modelled solar event and not otherwise.

tasks.title: Weather forecast API
tasks.detail: What the weather will be at a place and time. Flight planning, settlement shutters and mission generation all need to anticipate rather than react.
tasks.acceptance: A forecast issued six hours ahead matches what happens, within the model's stated confidence.

tasks.title: Volumetric performance budget
tasks.detail: Clouds, fog and precipitation are the easiest way to lose the frame. Resolution, temporal reprojection and distance-based quality, under one budget.
tasks.acceptance: Worst-case weather costs no more than 4 ms and degrades in detail rather than in frame rate.

tasks.title: Weather determinism and orbit-to-ground agreement
tasks.detail: Same seed and time gives the same weather, and the storm seen from orbit is the storm flown into.
tasks.acceptance: Both properties hold across a hundred sampled times and places.

tasks.title: Playable proof: fly into a storm front
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Visibility, wind loading and audio change together on entry, and the same storm is in the same place from orbit.

tasks.title: Ship definition format
tasks.detail: A ship is data: hull geometry, hardpoints, component slots, mass distribution, and the topology that connects them. Adding a ship must never require a compiler.
tasks.acceptance: A new ship is one data file plus art, and it flies.

tasks.title: Component graph with typed ports
tasks.detail: Components connect through typed ports — power, coolant, fuel, data — and the graph is what damage, heat and failure propagate through. This is the spine of the whole milestone.
tasks.acceptance: A component's inputs and outputs are discoverable at runtime and an unsatisfiable connection is a load error, not a crash.

tasks.title: Power generation and distribution
tasks.detail: Plants, buses, priorities and brownouts. Demand exceeding supply sheds load in priority order rather than stopping the ship.
tasks.acceptance: Overload a bus and the lowest-priority consumers drop first, in the order the configuration states.

tasks.title: Thermal model
tasks.detail: Components generate heat, coolant loops move it, radiators reject it, and an overheated component throttles or fails. Heat is also a signature.
tasks.acceptance: Run at full power with radiators retracted and the ship overheats on the schedule the thermal model predicts.

tasks.title: Fuel: types, tanks, transfer, consumption
tasks.detail: Propellant and reactor fuel as separate resources, consumed at rates the flight model produces rather than at a rate someone picked.
tasks.acceptance: Fuel burn integrated over a flight matches thrust integrated over the same flight, and running dry stops the engines.

tasks.title: Mass, centre of mass and inertia from contents
tasks.detail: Computed from hull, components, fuel and cargo, updating as fuel burns and cargo moves. An unevenly loaded ship handles unevenly.
tasks.acceptance: Load cargo on one side and the ship's handling changes measurably in the direction predicted.

tasks.title: Damage model over the component graph
tasks.detail: Hits damage components, damage propagates along ports, and the failure order is explained by the topology rather than by a table.
tasks.acceptance: Destroying a power coupling kills exactly the components downstream of it and nothing else.

tasks.title: Hull damage: penetration, deformation, breach
tasks.detail: Localised hull state, with pressure loss where the hull is breached and structural failure where enough of it is gone.
tasks.acceptance: A breach vents the compartment behind it and not the rest of the ship.

tasks.title: Component wear and condition
tasks.detail: Components degrade with use and with abuse, changing performance before they fail. The maintenance loop in M19 reads from this.
tasks.acceptance: A neglected thruster loses measurable output over a hundred hours of operation and warns before it fails.

tasks.title: Repair and component replacement
tasks.detail: Field repair with limited effect, workshop repair with full effect, and component swapping with the parts economy in mind.
tasks.acceptance: A damaged ship is repaired to a stated condition and the parts are consumed from somewhere.

tasks.title: Life support as a component
tasks.detail: Atmosphere, pressure and temperature inside the hull, with consumption, reserves and failure. On a breathable world it is a convenience; elsewhere it is the thing keeping you alive.
tasks.acceptance: Cut life support in vacuum and the internal atmosphere depletes on the modelled schedule, with warnings.

tasks.title: Shields
tasks.detail: Directional shields with capacity, recharge, and a power draw that competes with everything else on the bus.
tasks.acceptance: Raising shields measurably reduces power available to thrust, and the trade-off is visible on the instruments.

tasks.title: Signature model: thermal, electromagnetic, cross-section
tasks.detail: What a ship looks like to a sensor, derived from what it is doing. Running cold and quiet must be a real option, because information is the design's scarce commodity.
tasks.acceptance: Shutting down non-essential systems measurably reduces detection range, and the numbers come from the thermal and power models.

tasks.title: Hardpoints and mount framework
tasks.detail: The general mechanism for attaching things to a hull — weapons, mining gear, sensors, cargo pods — with size classes and power and cooling draw. Not the weapons themselves.
tasks.acceptance: A mount accepts any component of its class, refuses others, and its power and heat appear in the ship's totals.

tasks.title: Cargo hold and volumetric stowage
tasks.detail: Cargo occupies space and has mass and a position. A full hold is visibly full and an unbalanced one is felt.
tasks.acceptance: Loading to capacity is limited by volume or mass, whichever binds first, and the contents are visible in the hold.

tasks.title: Animated ship parts as components
tasks.detail: Gear, ramps, doors, radiators and canopies are components with state, power draw and failure modes, not animations.
tasks.acceptance: Cutting power mid-cycle leaves the gear half-deployed and it stays there until power returns.

tasks.title: Power-on and shutdown sequence
tasks.detail: A ship starts cold and comes up in an order the component graph implies. This is where a ship stops being a vehicle and becomes a machine.
tasks.acceptance: Cold start brings systems up in dependency order, and skipping a step prevents the next one.

tasks.title: Instrumentation framework
tasks.detail: Multi-function displays driven by real component state through one data path. An instrument that lies is a bug in the instrument, not in the display.
tasks.acceptance: Every gauge traces to a component reading, and a failed sensor makes its gauge unavailable rather than wrong.

tasks.title: Ship audio from component state
tasks.detail: Engine note from throttle and load, coolant pumps under thermal stress, alarms from the systems that raised them.
tasks.acceptance: A listener can identify which subsystem is in trouble from audio alone.

tasks.title: Damage visuals
tasks.detail: Scorching, deformation, venting, sparks and debris tied to the damage state rather than played as effects.
tasks.acceptance: A ship's exterior condition is readable at a glance and matches its component state.

tasks.title: Ship configuration and outfitting
tasks.detail: Swap components within slot and power constraints, with the consequences computed rather than listed.
tasks.acceptance: Fitting an oversized power plant changes mass, heat and handling, and the configuration screen shows all three before it is fitted.

tasks.title: Ship state persistence
tasks.detail: Condition, fuel, cargo, damage and configuration survive a save, a reload and eventually a handover to the simulation.
tasks.acceptance: A damaged, half-fuelled, oddly configured ship reloads exactly as it was.

tasks.title: Ship diagnostics and test harness
tasks.detail: A headless rig that builds a ship, applies loads and damage, and asserts the component graph behaves. Ship bugs are systemic and need systemic tests.
tasks.acceptance: Every failure mode in this milestone has a test that reproduces it without flying anything.

tasks.title: Playable proof: shoot out a power coupling
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Thrusters on that bus go dead, heat climbs, systems degrade in graph order, and repair brings the ship back.

tasks.title: Rigid-body integration with a real inertia tensor
tasks.detail: Replace the prototype's hand-integrated point mass with a proper rigid body using the mass distribution M05 computes. Still hand-integrated rather than handed to Chaos, for the reasons in SS6.9.
tasks.acceptance: Angular response matches the inertia tensor, and an off-axis thrust produces the torque the geometry predicts.

tasks.title: Thruster allocation solver
tasks.detail: Given thruster positions, orientations and limits, solve for the combination producing the commanded force and torque. This is what makes a ship's handling a consequence of its thruster layout rather than of a handling number.
tasks.acceptance: Disable a thruster and the solver compensates, with the loss of authority in the axis the geometry predicts.

tasks.title: Flight assist and control modes
tasks.detail: Assist on, assist off, coupled and decoupled, each a different controller over the same allocator rather than a different flight model.
tasks.acceptance: Switching modes changes only the controller; the physics underneath is identical and provably so.

tasks.title: Aerodynamics: lift, drag and control surfaces
tasks.detail: Real aerodynamic forces from angle of attack, airspeed and the atmospheric density M04 provides, with control surfaces that only work in air.
tasks.acceptance: A winged ship glides unpowered in atmosphere and does not in vacuum.

tasks.title: Stall, spin and recovery
tasks.detail: An aerodynamic envelope with edges. Exceeding them has consequences that can be recovered from if the pilot knows how.
tasks.acceptance: A deliberate stall departs controlled flight and standard recovery inputs recover it.

tasks.title: Vacuum-to-atmosphere transition
tasks.detail: Aerodynamic authority fades in as density rises and thruster authority does not, so the handover is continuous rather than a mode change.
tasks.acceptance: A re-entry from vacuum to sea level shows no discontinuity in forces at any altitude.

tasks.title: VTOL and hover
tasks.detail: Vertical thrust with ground effect, and the fuel cost that makes hovering a decision rather than a default.
tasks.acceptance: Hovering consumes fuel at the rate thrust-to-weight implies, and ground effect is measurable near the surface.

tasks.title: Landing gear and ground handling
tasks.detail: Suspension, contact, friction, braking and steering on the ground. Landing is a physical event, not a state change.
tasks.acceptance: A hard landing compresses the gear and can damage it; a shallow one does not; the ship stays put on a slope up to the friction limit.

tasks.title: G-force model and pilot effects
tasks.detail: Sustained and transient acceleration on the pilot, with the visual and physiological limits that make manoeuvres have a cost.
tasks.acceptance: A sustained high-g turn greys the view on the modelled schedule and recovery follows the same model.

tasks.title: Flight computer limits and envelope protection
tasks.detail: Configurable limits on the allocator — g, angular rate, thermal — that a pilot can relax at their own risk.
tasks.acceptance: Limits are enforced by the controller, and disabling them lets the airframe be damaged.

tasks.title: Autopilot framework
tasks.detail: Hold attitude, hold altitude, hold station, approach and auto-land, as controllers over the same allocator. Directives in M21 will drive ships through this.
tasks.acceptance: Auto-land puts a ship on a pad in wind, repeatably, from any approach.

tasks.title: Docking
tasks.detail: Approach corridors, alignment, capture and release against a station or another ship, with the moving-frame handover M08 will formalise.
tasks.acceptance: Dock with a station in orbit and the ship's frame becomes the station's with no jolt.

tasks.title: Ground vehicle framework
tasks.detail: Wheeled and tracked vehicles over the same rigid body and the same terrain collision, because a settlement needs things that are not ships.
tasks.acceptance: A ground vehicle drives across terrain with suspension responding to the surface the renderer draws.

tasks.title: Input framework: HOTAS, gamepad, mouse and keyboard
tasks.detail: One binding layer over one command set, with curves, deadzones and per-device profiles. Not three control schemes.
tasks.acceptance: All three devices produce identical commanded forces for equivalent input, and rebinding requires no code.

tasks.title: HUD and flight instruments
tasks.detail: Velocity vector, attitude, target reticle, energy, and the instruments a pilot actually flies on — driven through M05's instrumentation path.
tasks.acceptance: A full flight is completable on instruments alone with the external view disabled.

tasks.title: Collision response for vehicles
tasks.detail: Impacts transfer momentum and damage components through M05's graph, rather than triggering a generic effect.
tasks.acceptance: A glancing impact damages the components at the point of contact and imparts the momentum the collision implies.

tasks.title: Ship-to-ship physical interaction
tasks.detail: Ships push each other, land on each other, and carry each other. The prerequisite for M08's nested frames.
tasks.acceptance: A small ship lands on a large one and is carried with it.

tasks.title: Flight recorder
tasks.detail: Record every input, force and state to a file that can be replayed exactly. Flight bugs are transient and unreproducible without this.
tasks.acceptance: A recorded flight replays to an identical trajectory.

tasks.title: Flight model tuning tools
tasks.detail: In-editor visualisation of thruster authority, aerodynamic forces, envelope and control response, so tuning is measured rather than felt.
tasks.acceptance: A ship's envelope can be read off a chart the tool generates.

tasks.title: Flight regression suite
tasks.detail: Recorded flights replayed in CI with trajectory tolerances, so a physics change that alters handling is caught immediately.
tasks.acceptance: A deliberate one-percent thrust change fails the suite.

tasks.title: Playable proof: continent, orbit, pad
tasks.detail: Rule 6. The gate, run and recorded.
tasks.acceptance: Pad to another continent aerodynamically, out to vacuum, manoeuvre, re-enter with heating, land on the pad you left — cockpit only.

tasks.title: Origin rebasing
tasks.detail: Move the world under the camera so float precision never has to express an astronomical unit. The prototype avoids this by keeping vertices patch-relative; everything else in the game will not have that luxury.
tasks.acceptance: At one AU from origin, a one-millimetre movement is still one millimetre, for every actor and every particle system.

tasks.title: Depth precision across twelve orders of magnitude
tasks.detail: A cockpit instrument at 40 cm and a planet at 400,000 km in one frame. Reversed-Z with cascaded depth ranges, or a logarithmic buffer, chosen by measurement rather than by preference.
tasks.acceptance: No z-fighting anywhere from a hand-held object to a planet on the same screen.

tasks.title: Scale-aware camera and rendering
